#6081. I Flew A United Airlines Boeing 737 MAX From A Remote Island Airport With Just 2 Weekly Flights: Here's What It Was Like

From its regional hub in Guam, United Airlines is the only airline that provides regular air connections to some of the small Micronesian islands in the Pacific. Flying on some of these routes is a memorable experience, with local airports operating a TSA- and FAA-compliant system on sleepy little islands. Some island airports only wake up for a flight every second day. In November 2026, I flew from the island of Yap (a state in the Federated States of Micronesia or FSM) to Guam on board a United flight.

One of the most notable regional flight connections United offers is the famous Island Hopper, which flies from Guam to Chuuk, Pohnpei, Kosrae, Kwajalein, Majuro, and Honolulu, and back again. I wanted to take this flight to Majuro, but it was beyond my budget. Some United Micronesia flights operate only twice a week, meaning the flight schedule dictates the tour schedule. On the upside, many of these Micronesian flights routinely operate half-full, meaning booking out is unusual for certain routes.

Describing island hopping in Micronesia with United is often much more about the experience at the airport than with United itself. Yap International Airport is served only by United flights (with 737s) twice a week from Guam and by Pacific Missionary Aviation's (PMA) Beechcraft Super King Air 200 flights (with seven to nine passengers) once a week from Palau. PMA is set to introduce a second weekly flight next year.

As these are Yap's only regularly scheduled passenger flights, the airport is generally otherwise closed. I flew from Palau to Yap with PMA and then to Guam with United Airlines. As explained below, PMA offers the only scheduled passenger access to Yap for those who cannot pass through US immigration.

There are no direct flights connecting the State of Yap with the three other far-flung states of Chuuk, Pohnpei, and Kosrae​​​​​. To access those other islands and avoid United (and US immigration), the main alternative is Nauru Airlines. United's flight from Yap to Guam departs at 2:30 am, arriving in Guam at around 4:00 am, making it difficult to decide whether to book a hotel for the night before, the night of, or not at all. I opted not to book.

The experience of checking into United's various island flights differs significantly by island and airport. Some airports (especially on Saipan) are much larger and more sophisticated than Yap, but Yap was the one I flew through, and so I will describe that one here. Yap's check-in and baggage drop-off facilities are located in a covered area outside the building. During the check-in process, there is no air conditioning.

At the baggage drop-off (positioned before check-in), the staff informed me that their equipment was broken, so my bag would be manually searched. Many of the bags being checked in for the flight were wares in basic boxes and containers by locals to sell on other islands. Check-in was straightforward, with me presenting my current passport and my expired passport with the US visa.

One of the notable features of Yap is that the country does not collect the exit fee in the airfare. There is a window where passengers must pay the $20 exit fee before going to the adjacent immigration window. These two windows are located on the outside of the airport. After stamping the passport out of the country, there is nothing in principle to stop passengers from walking away into the night, away from the airport. Passengers wait outside the airport until the security check opens.

The carrier has launched new flights from Tokyo Narita Airport.

Even though the United flight was at most half full, perhaps a third, the entire check-in and security process was rather slow. This was particularly true of the security check. It appeared that the TSA had a representative at the station to oversee the security check, although I didn't ask, and I'm unsure. Security was one of the slowest I've seen in the world, perhaps the slowest.

Only after the security check do passengers move into the airport's only waiting room with the sole boarding gate. Located outside the airport terminal is a very basic shop selling some snacks; inside the airport terminal, there is none. The turnaround time for United flights is slow compared with main airports. The Boeing 737 MAX 8 touches down at 1:10 AM and departs at 2:35 AM.

Yap Airport lacks a Passenger Boarding Bridge (PBB) and a shuttle bus. Passengers walk from the terminal to the aircraft parked on the apron. The flight was perhaps around a third booked. I asked the local passenger next to me, and he said the flight is typically half empty. That United flight is the primary connection for Yapese, whose population is made up of around 7,000 people on the main island and 4,000 on the outer islands.

Being a modern international US airport, Guam International Airport is dramatically different from Yap. One of the most notable features of the airport is its lack of a transit area, requiring all connecting passengers to pass through US immigration. I was visiting Guam for two days, so I planned to go through immigration anyway. Due to my travel record (which includes Iran, Somalia, Pakistan, among other countries), I was questioned by CBP for three hours.

While Guam is not a particularly large airport, it is large enough to feel like a large international airport, especially after visiting remote Pacific airports. Renting cars is straightforward and easy, with my rental only requiring a $100 security deposit and not requiring a credit card. From Guam, passengers can island hop with United to Palau, the Northern Mariana Islands, the FSM, the Marshall Islands, Hawaii, and various other mainstream destinations (e.g., Japan, Taiwan).

United Airlines' Island Hopper Destinations (per United)

United is the only mainline US airline operating at Guam with a near-monopoly (99%) on local, regional, and US routes. According to the airport's report, United operated 87 weekly flights to 14 destinations over the greater region in 2024. The airport is also served by a number of Asian international carriers, including Japan Airlines, Korean Air, Jin Air, Philippine Airlines, and Air Busan. I flew out on Philippine Airlines.

The airline deploys its largest aircraft across its network, but San Francisco sees it the most.

I flew on a new United Boeing MAX 8 (registered N37319) that was delivered in 2023. The airliner is currently tasked with island-hopping routes in the region, including the Island Hopper itself. Other recent destinations include Osaka, Tokyo, and Manila. No food or refreshments are served on the Yap to Guam flight, whose flight time is around one hour and ten minutes. The lack of refreshments is perhaps welcome, as that hour was the only time I got all night to close my eyes.

While the flight is technically an international flight, in terms of aircraft allocation and configuration, United treats it as a domestic flight. The MAX 8 is configured in a two-class layout. It is fitted with 16 United First (domestic business class) seats and 150 economy class seats (including Economy Plus) for a total of 166 seats. The seats are comfortable for economy. Overall, United's economy class seems to be roughly equivalent to some higher-end, low-cost Asian carriers like AirAsia.

There is in-seat entertainment as well as in-seat charging (USB and power outlets). Perhaps due to the low capacity and the lack of competition, United's fares to Micronesian islands are typically expensive, with hops between islands often costing more than flights to destinations in Asia. As United has a monopoly in some cases, there is little choice but to accept the fares.

United Airlines dominates the international and main route connections of the island nations of Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia, and the Marshall Islands, along with the US territories of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands. This is largely a legacy of the American administration of the former Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands (TTPI) that it inherited after WWII, having conquered the islands from Japan. Eventually, the TTPI broke up and became three independent nation-states and the US Northern Mariana Commonwealth.

United is effectively the commercial successor to Air Micronesia. Air Micronesia was set up in 1968 by Continental Airlines, Aloha Airlines, and the United Micronesian Development Association. It connected the various main islands with Guam and other regional destinations. For the region, this was a major development as the islands previously lacked a viable alternative. Later on, the airline was rebranded as Continental Micronesia with Guam as its main operating hub. In time, the Trust Territory broke up, but none of the succeeding countries was large enough to sustain its own national airline providing higher-end air services.

The volume of passenger traffic is also small, leading to United flights often flying partially empty, meaning there is little scope to accommodate two competing airlines. In 2010, United Airlines merged with Continental Airlines, with the two integrating their operations. In 2017, the legacy Continental Micronesia separate operating certificate was retired, leaving the core United brand alone.

#6080. New FAA Rule For Planes Lining Up On Runways May Cause Delays

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some new restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance. This is intended to add an extra safety buffer, but to quote an airline pilot on an ATC frequency, “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”

As of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a new rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports. Air traffic controllers want to utilize runways as efficiently as possible for both takeoffs and landings, and that often involves having planes line up on the runway and wait, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.

To give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart. In those situations, it’s common for the air traffic controller to clear that next plane to “line up and wait.”

The idea is that the plane then has clearance to enter the runway, and then await further takeoff clearance. After all, it might take 30 seconds or so for a plane to taxi from the hold short point of the runway, to getting into position on the runway.

Under the new FAA rules, air traffic controllers will only be allowed to clear pilots to “line up and wait” in situations where there’s a dedicated supervisor or controller-in-charge who can’t perform other duties while these operations are underway. In the past this was a recommendation, but now this is a rule.

Given constant air traffic control staffing shortages, this could actually impact operations a good percentage of the time. Here’s how the reason for this policy change is described:

The core purpose of this change is to elevate the safety standard for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations by removing ambiguity in staffing requirements. By upgrading the guidance from “should” (a recommendation) to “must” (a mandatory requirement), the FAA ensures that the personnel providing watch supervision (OS/CIC) are fully dedicated to overseeing the safety of the operation without the distraction of simultaneously managing other operational tasks.

I can appreciate the concept behind this, which is to improve safety. After all, we have air traffic controllers who are spread too thin, and all too often, they get a bit distracted due to the volume of things they have to deal with. That has definitely been a contributing factor to many accidents and incidents over the years.

I do find the timing of this being introduced to be interesting, as it comes during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. I don’t think this will actually lead to any major issues, and for that matter, safety shouldn’t be compromised just because flights are busy.

If you’re an observant passenger who is always looking out the window and is on Flightradar24, you may notice this policy in practice, for situations where you feel like the plane should already be lining up on the runway, but isn’t.

I can’t imagine this policy change will lead to any major delays on a widespread basis, but then again, given how at capacity many airports are, even a little change can make a big difference. Below you can hear some talk between an air traffic controller at Albuquerque Airport (ABQ) and a Southwest pilot, where they’re discussing the change. As you can hear, the pilot says “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”

A new FAA runway safety requirement takes effect across the United States tomorrow, November 24, and an air traffic controller in Albuquerque is already warning pilots about possible delays.The change requires airports to have a dedicated supervisor on duty before controllers… pic.twitter.com/zxXariHNAy

While the FAA is making changes intended to improve safety, how about also requiring air traffic controllers in the United States to start using standard phraseology, like everywhere else in the world? 😉

As of today, the FAA has added a new restriction on planes being able to line up on runways. A “line up and wait” procedure is pretty standard, but will now only be allowed in situations where the air traffic controller is only focused on one thing. Given how short staffed air traffic control often is, this could have some implications.

I don’t think this will meaningfully slow things down on a national level, but for airports that make the most of every second to get planes in and out, it could definitely have implications.

What do you make of the FAA’s new restrictions on takeoff?

#6079. Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

#6078. BermudAir Adding Flights All Over The Place: I Don’t Know What’s Going On

BermudAir, the unusual boutique carrier that launched operations a few years back, keeps getting stranger. The company has just announced a massive expansion for the summer of 2027, and with this, we’ll see the airline add all kinds of seemingly random routes to and from Bermuda, plus all kinds of routes that don’t touch Bermuda.

Whether you want to fly from Nashville to Ocho Rios, or from Fredericton to Bermuda, the airline now has you covered!

For a little bit of background, in mid-2023 we saw the launch of BermudAir, a quirky niche airline with the goal of operating Embraer jets between Bermuda (BDA) and the United States and Canada. Initially the airline was going to operate all-business class planes, but it scrapped (“delayed”) that concept before launch, instead introducing a two-cabin concept (though business class just has blocked adjacent seats and better service).

As I said from the beginning, the whole thing struck me as an odd venture, essentially trying to serve Bermuda year-round profitably, while going up against the major carriers that serve the airport.

To my surprise, the airline is still in business over three years after launch, though it hasn’t necessarily been that smooth. As is pretty common for an airlines startup, the first years have been rocky, with several routes being cut after launch. For that matter, the airline faced a lawsuit over millions in unpaid airport fees at its hub, which isn’t exactly a great sign.

Several months back, BermudAir announced new winter 2026-2027 seasonal flying to places other than Bermuda. Now the airline has announced summer seasonal flying for 2027, and it’s arguably even stranger. The routes are all over the place.

In the summer of 2027, BermudAir will fly from Bermuda (BDA) to the following destinations:

On top of that, the airline will be expanding beyond Bermuda, with new seasonal services in the following markets:

Below is BermudAir’s updated map with destinations listed…

I really can’t make sense of what is going on at BermudAir. I feel like we’ve had reasons to be suspicious, when you look at the initial business model, vs. how things have played out:

I’m not suggesting there’s no demand in any of these new markets. The demand may very well be there. But there are a lot of challenges here:

What’s interesting here is how the airline announced seems to be taking a similar strategy both for this winter and for next summer. So based on the fact that the airline is moving forward with its current winter schedule, maybe this is working? I don’t know…

It’s also interesting how the airline actually got permission to operate these routes. As a reminder, Bermuda, Anguilla, and Turks & Caicos, are all British Overseas Territories, and Belize and Jamaica are former British Overseas Territory. How does the airline get permission to serve places like Honduras, though? I guess the airline is somehow getting permission to operate this as fifth freedom service, or something.

BermudAir is expanding rapidly, as the airline has announced new routes for the summer of 2027. Not only does this include several new routes to Bermuda (including out of Fredericton!), but the airline is also adding flying between the United States and Grand Cayman, Honduras, Jamaica, etc.

I think BermudAir deserves an award for the most unusual route network of any “real” airline. I certainly can’t think of any other airline in this “league.”

What do you make of BermudAir’s latest expansion?

#6077. LATAM Refused My Refund Within 24 Hours, And The Reason Makes No Sense

Over the weekend, I booked an expensive ticket for my dad, brother, and me, from Buenos Aires (EZE) to Santiago (SCL), only to come across a better deal after I’d booked. I called customer service to cancel within the 24-hour cooling-off period, but was refused a refund for the most convoluted and unnecessary reason.

LATAM is the airline I’ve flown with the second most in my life after British Airways, my old home airline. It’s an airline I look forward to flying with for several reasons. However, this recent booking experience has uncovered a gaping hole in its customer service, which in the air I’ve always found to be excellent.

This whole situation could have been avoided if I’d been able to pay with my UK credit card on LATAM’s Brazilian website.

The Brazilian site has no issue when entering UK credit card details.

However, the default setting for postcodes (ZIP codes) is numerical-only because, as in the US, Brazil’s postcodes consist only of numbers. In the UK, they’re made up of letters and numbers, so I couldn’t add the postcode that my credit card is registered to.

I tried using only the numbers of my postcode (the one in the example above is random), but the site returned an error, saying it failed to connect to my bank. My guess would be this wouldn’t be a problem for US credit cards, given that ZIP codes consist only of numbers too.

I remember this happening previously, but I never had an issue with a booking that I couldn’t change online.

Ideally, I would have paid with a Brazilian bank account or credit card, but I’m still working through the immigration bureaucracy required to open one.

First of all, I tried to cancel by logging into my LATAM Pass account, but was redirected to the contact center. This is when I realized how much of an obstacle my booking via the UK website would be.

After being put on hold 3 times for what seemed like forever, the agent I spoke with at LATAM’s Brazilian call center told me there was nothing she could do to help me.

She explained the only way I’d get a refund was to call the UK call center, since I’d paid in GBP on the UK website. I called just before the cut-off of the 24-hour cooling-off period, so by then I had exceeded it. I had only left it so close to the cooling-off period because I was researching the trip again the following day and found a better deal; otherwise, I wouldn’t have wanted to cancel.

If I had called sooner and had more time, I could have asked someone in the UK to call for me, as my Brazilian phone number can’t make outgoing international calls. I did top up my UK SIM Card with 20 GBP, but at a charge of 2 GBP per minute, the call disconnected after 10 minutes on hold with no answer.

Irrespective of whether I could have found an easier way to contact the UK call center, I can’t help but feel that my issue should have been resolved there and then over the phone by the Brazilian call center agent. After all, I booked directly through the airline’s website, and then called the airline directly to cancel. It makes no logical sense!

Because of a stupidly convoluted system, I’m stuck with a LATAM ticket that I can no longer cancel, even though I called customer service within the 24-hour cooling-off period.

It’s not the end of the world, as we can still take the flights we’d originally booked, but it’s so frustrating to be put in a situation like this in 2026 because of such an archaic technicality.

I’m still a big fan of LATAM itself, and will continue to fly it, at least until my Platinum status runs out next year.

What’s the most frustrating post-sale customer service experience you’ve had?

I’m Canadian and Brazilian and this has helped me lots of times to use my Canadian credit card on Brazilian and US websites.

All these rude people attacking Daniel when all he wanted to do was alert people so that we can be more careful if we are in the same situation. #6076. Mississippi Cessna 210 Crash Kills 6 After 10,000-Foot/Minute Descent

A Cessna 210 Centurion six-seat light aircraft crashed into the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Horn Island after descending at 10,000 feet (3,050 meters) per minute. All six passengers tragically died in the crash, including four adults and two boys, aged eight and 10.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) have started an investigation into the accident. The NTSB will lead this work and provide updates as more information becomes available.

The Cessna involved in the crash took off from New Orleans at 2:00 PM local time and was bound for Fort Myers, Florida, with the tail number N29002. At 3:45 PM, the regional air traffic control tower in Mobile, Alabama, reported losing contact with the aircraft. WVUE, a New Orleans news station, has reported that those onboard were traveling back home after enjoying a fishing trip in Venice, Louisiana.

Coast Guard responders began searching the waters over which the aircraft had been flying. They found only three life jackets, an unoccupied life raft, and the plane's floating cabin. Divers then went into the Gulf of Mexico and recovered the bodies of all of those onboard.

Commander Trevor Blount, the coordinator for the Coast Guard's search-and-rescue operations in the Mobile area, spoke about the efforts.

"We are grateful for the strong inter-agency coordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families."

The FAA and NTSB have started their investigation into the accident. Some information has already emerged. For example, the Coast Guard has said the aircraft was falling at a rate of 10,000 feet (3,050 meters) per minute when it crashed. The FAA's database shows that the aircraft is registered to EAB Services, which is based in Cape Coral, Florida. It was active for the past week, safely completing a few trips.

This included Fort Myers to Buras, Louisiana on November 21, and Fort Myers to East Rutherfordton, North Carolina (outbound and return) on November 19.

Simple Flying has contacted the FAA, which confirmed the incident in a statement.

"A Cessna 210 crashed southwest of Pascagoula, Mississippi, around 3:30 PM. local time on Tuesday, Nov. 24. Six people were on board. The FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board will investigate. The NTSB will lead the investigation and provide any updates."

The accident occurred after the aircraft attempted to divert while en route to Austin.

Cessna accidents and incidents made headlines earlier this week. An Air Canada Boeing 737 MAX 8 received a Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) alert because of an unresponsive Cessna in close proximity. The 737 MAX was climbing out of Palm Springs International Airport (PSP) and bound for Vancouver International Airport (YVR).

The pilots received a resolution advisory at approximately 11,400 feet (3,500 meters) to climb an additional 600 feet (183 meters), allowing the two planes to reach a safe amount of separation. Luckily, the two aircraft were kept apart from each other. However, the Cessna's identity and the minimum distance that separated the two aircraft remains unclear. The Air Canada jet safely completed its journey to Vancouver, which took two hours and 40 minutes.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Few things compare to seeing the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in person on a crisp November morning. Watching massive balloons float down the streets of New York City is an iconic holiday experience on many families’ travel wish lists.

Assuming you don’t live near the Big Apple, seeing the parade may require forgoing (or delaying) a traditional Thanksgiving meal at home. However, it will likely be well worth the effort once you see your child giddy with excitement as their favorite cartoon characters float by to the tune of a marching band in full regalia, while giant floats with entertainers glide by at street level.

Note, though, that more than 3.5 million people attend the parade in person each year. It’s important to strategize your visit so you are not far from the curb, struggling to catch a glimpse of the street.

There are several things you’ll want to keep in mind as you plan your day at the parade. Here are our top tips for viewing the 100th annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in 2026.

If you want to get an up-close view of the balloons featured in the annual parade, you won’t want to miss the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Balloon Inflation. The inflation occurs the day before the parade, starting at 1 p.m. on the Upper West Side at 72nd Street and Columbus Avenue, near the American Museum of Natural History. It runs until 6 p.m., so you have several hours to sneak a peek at what’s to come during the parade. (Tip: The line opens at noon.)

There are 32 balloons that will transform from flat to fully inflated during the course of the afternoon. There are some fun new floats to keep an eye out for this year. To name a few, Bob the Minion riding a giant banana, Sorcerer Mickey, the Geico gecko and Earl the Squirrel, a balloon based on a real-life squirrel who made his home in Universal Orlando's Christmas tree several years ago and has now become the park's official holiday mascot.

Inflating a giant balloon the height of a four-story building takes time. Long lines form as the balloons become fully inflated in the early evening, so you may want to test your luck by arriving closer to 3 p.m., when most of the balloons start taking shape.

To get to the event location via public transportation, allow extra time; the subway station at 72nd Street tends to get very crowded as the afternoon wears on. You can also hail a cab or use a ride-hailing service, though you’ll want to be dropped off a block or two north of the gated-off section to avoid delays. Once you're in the line, you'll progress north and can exit west along any block from West 82nd to West 86th streets.

TPG tip: The closest subway station to the entrance point is the B and C stop at 72nd Street and Central Park West. Consider taking the 1, 2 or 3 train to Broadway and 72nd Street instead. It’s a few blocks west but an easy walk — just follow the crowds.

Related: These are the best New York City hotels for families to check out

Some parade-goers arrive as early as 4 a.m. to snag a coveted front-row spot along the route.

Plan accordingly if you have a particular location in mind. For example, prime seats at covered bus stops start filling up around 4 a.m., while you might be able to get front-row curb seating closer to 6 a.m.

Should you have deeper pockets and want to avoid being outside in the elements, you can pay for a parade brunch with a view along the parade route. Just be sure to make these reservations well in advance, as they tend to fill up quickly. Or, of course, you could book a room with a view directly on the parade route.

For those arriving later in the morning, you can stand in the closed-off side streets leading to the parade. You might be 10-15 people back, but you can still see most of the action.

The parade starts at 8:30 a.m. at Central Park West on 77th Street. Since the route is 2.5 miles long, it can take close to an hour for the lead marchers to reach Macy's. This means you’ll have some idle time before you can start watching the spectacle.

Because you could find yourself waiting several hours for the parade to show up, you’ll want to bring some stuff to stay occupied, like snacks, drinks and games. A backup charger is also a good idea.

You can bring camping chairs, buckets or anything else you may want to sit on to the parade, though these items are not very helpful for the parade itself, since most people stand. Still, at the very least, you’ll probably want to have some hotel towels or blankets to sit on instead of the hard, cold, gum-covered New York City sidewalks.

Don’t forget proper attire, including jackets, hats, gloves and umbrellas if rain is in the forecast, since the weather can turn quickly in late fall.

Like at home, excitement builds as the parade start time nears, and before long, cheers erupt as the parade comes into view. However, what you may not realize from watching at home is how interactive the experience can be. You may get high-fives from clowns and even confetti in your hair.

Not everything you see on TV happens along the parade route, either. Some performances, including those by the Radio City Rockettes and various singing and dance groups, only occur in front of Macy’s Herald Square (where the cameras are). As a result, you’ll want to manage your expectations. Don’t worry about what you’re missing. Instead, focus on all that’s taking place in front of you: the floats, balloons and festivities.

Related: 10 tips for flying during the holidays

The parade covers so much of the city that there isn’t one best hotel for attending the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. While some hotels are physically on the parade route, it’s not as simple as booking a room at one of these properties and watching the festivities from your window.

Sure, some windows at the route-adjacent hotels offer good views — but hotels are savvy, so those rooms are often sold as part of pricier parade packages. As such, you’ll have to pay more and often meet minimum stay requirements to see the parade from your actual hotel room.

If you don’t want to splurge to see all the action from your room, ask if your hotel has a special viewing area for guests. Often, hotels on the parade route have some space outside where patrons can watch the parade as it passes.

A few properties on the parade route include:

Should you have trouble securing a room at a property on the parade route or wish to save a little money, consider staying a block or more off the route at properties like The St. Regis New York and Park Hyatt New York. Both are a very short walk to and from the parade.

Some more points-friendly hotels that are within walking distance of the parade route include:

Related: 10 festive hotels for people who really love the holidays

Since New York City is an incredible place to be for the holidays, there are all kinds of other ways to celebrate the season after kicking it off with the parade. Be sure to see Santa in person at Santaland on the eighth floor of Macy’s on 34th Street (reservations are required). The Big Apple Circus, under the big top in Lincoln Center, is a sure-fire family pleaser. Also, peruse some of the festive holiday markets throughout the city when you’re not busy ice skating at Rockefeller Center or catching a performance of a Christmas classic like “The Nutcracker” or “A Christmas Carol.”

#6073. Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

“This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

“We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

“I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

#6072. Orient Express Sailing Yachts Review: Corinthian’s Suites, Dining, Amenities, Service, And More

For the main event of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, Ford and I had the chance to spend four nights on the Corinthian, which is the first ship in Orient Express’ new cruising venture, known as Orient Express Sailing Yachts.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts set sail in the summer of 2026, and with just 54 suites that can accommodate up to 110 guests, it really brings luxury cruising to a new level. It’s a fascinating time for the luxury cruising industry more broadly, given how competition has been heating up.

I also recently reviewed Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, and had a great experience, and reviewed Four Seasons Yachts, which is definitely more luxurious, but also has some growing pains. Lastly, I’ve compared all the experiences as well.

While Orient Express Sailing Yachts is the highest priced cruising venture to date, I have to say, the experience really is unbelievably good, and at least you feel like you’re getting an amazing experience. I come into these kinds of trips with a critical eye, and I was just blown away by the ship’s design, the quality of the food and drinks, and the service. To me the ship felt like a step back in time (in terms of its classic elegance), while also being cutting edge modern.

If you can swing this experience, I’d highly recommend it. Okay, enough of an intro, here comes my 8,500-word review (yikes, this is the longest review I’ve ever published of anything).

Orient Express Sailing Yachts charges per suite (rather than per person, based on double occupancy), and you’ll find that journeys typically cost an average of $4,000-6,000 per cabin per night for a base suite. Make no mistake, this is the very top end of the cruise market, and at this point you’re paying safari prices for the experience.

Let me also emphasize that rates go up from there, and Orient Express Sailing Yachts has some of the most insane suites you’ll find at sea, some of which can cost six figures per sailing. Currently, Orient Express offers cruises in Europe in summer, and in the Caribbean in winter, with transatlantic sailings in the spring and fall.

For what it’s worth, you’ll find rate parity regardless of which booking channel you reserve through. So your best bet is to book through a travel advisor affiliated with Accor Preferred, because they can add perks to your journey. The size of the credit depends on the accommodation type booked, plus the length of the journey.

In the interest of full disclosure, Ford was invited on this Orient Express Sailing Yachts journey (due to the amount of volume he books), and I tagged along with him. All opinions expressed are my own, and I plan to review this exactly the same way I reviewed the two previous cruises (which we paid full price for). I haven’t been asked to write anything, and I have no incentive to be anything other than honest. If people are going to drop a ton of money on a luxury cruise, I want to make sure they’re at least getting the best experience possible.

We experienced Orient Express Sailing Yachts in early October 2026, shortly before the ship’s transatlantic sailing. Admittedly it wasn’t the most exciting itinerary, but that’s just what worked out for us in terms of timing, since we wanted to minimize our time away from home, had to schedule it around when family could best be with our kids, etc. Below is the itinerary for the sailing we took.

We were happy with this itinerary, since our primary goal was to see the ship. It definitely wasn’t the most exciting, though, given that we docked at the port in Mahón (rather than tendering), and it also meant we didn’t have a marina day (not that you’d necessarily want that in October, since it’s a bit chillier). But the point is that if you’re traveling more in peak season, you can expect a marina day more consistently.

Historically, cruising has been all about offering an all-inclusive experience. That’s true with Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, but then Four Seasons Yachts countered the trend, by only including breakfast, and then charging extra for lunch, dinner, and drinks (I don’t love this concept, especially given the quality issues they have).

While Orient Express Sailing Yachts might charge a lot, what I really appreciate is how the company has an ultra all-inclusive concept, to an extent that’s even greater than you’ll find on most other cruise lines. Orient Express Sailing Yachts journeys include the following:

Orient Express Sailing Yachts journeys don’t include the following:

Regarding the Orient Express Sailing Yachts tipping policy, the company states that gratuities are included in the fare — “however, if you wish to offer a tip as an extra gesture of appreciation, it will be warmly received.”

I just have to emphasize that the level of inclusions really impressed me. Seriously, I was served caviar with breakfast, lunch, and dinner at various points (and even cocktails!), and the house champagne is Veuve Clicquot La Grande Dame 2018 (which retails for around $200 per bottle).

Orient Express Sailing Yachts currently has a single ship, which is named the Corinthian (a second ship is being introduced in 2027, and it’ll be named the Olympian).

The ship entered service in 2026, and is 722 feet (220 meters) long, 82 feet (25 meters) wide, and 26,600 gross tons. With 54 accommodations and a maximum capacity of around 110 guests, there’s a roughly 1.5:1 staff to guest ratio, given that there are around 170 staff onboard. The spaciousness of this ship, and the amount of space allocated to each passenger, really is next level.

The Corinthian also has the title of being the world’s largest sailing yacht, as it has three automated SolidSail rigid sails on tilting carbon masts, to provide wind propulsion, alongside hybrid LNG auxiliary power. It’s just such an elegant and distinctive looking ship, that it can’t help but turn heads. For those curious, it was explained that the sails reduce emissions by around 10%, and no, the ship doesn’t “heel” in the way a smaller sailboat would. Unless you’re looking up, you wouldn’t realize there are even sails.

You can find the full Corinthian deck plan here. As you’d expect for a sail boat, there aren’t quite as many floors as on a traditional cruise ship. Guests can access a total of five floors, between levels three and seven. To briefly cover that:

Near the ship’s entrance, you’ll find a very cool directory of sorts, which shows the floorplan of the ship. You can click any amenity, and then it will light up, so that’s super handy.

The ship has two sets of elevator banks, as well as two sets of staircases, so getting around the ship is really easy. We always used the stairs, since we were typically within a couple of floors of where we needed to be.

As you’d expect, the ease of boarding a ship varies greatly depending on its size, but Orient Express Sailing Yachts really took it to the next level in terms of how seamless it was. We had spent a night at the Hôtel Dieu Intercontinental Marseille. Our journey included the transfers, so an Orient Express representative met us at the hotel, and then we were driven to the port.

Getting onboard the ship literally couldn’t have been easier. There were no formalities in the port, but instead, we were escorted straight through security, and then check-in was handled once onboard.

There were no other guests as we boarded, and the staff really went above and beyond — for example, the crew member who escorted us through security and onto the ship insisted on holding an umbrella over our heads, to shade us from the sun.

Our check-in process onboard took all of five minutes, and at that point we were introduced to our butler, Reuben, who escorted us to our suite, and took care of everything from there. I should mention how Reuben was German, so they specifically appointed us a German butler, which I thought was super fun (so we communicated with him exclusively in German).

We didn’t have a stop that involved tendering, but for those situations where you do, it’s an efficient process, given how few guests there are. Our one stop had us docked in port, and there was a nice seating area outside the ship with bottled water, sunscreen, etc. Admittedly a setup like this is more useful when you’re waiting on a tender, rather than just walking directly onto or off the ship.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts has 54 suites onboard, spread across over a dozen different categories. The entry level suites here are among the most spacious at sea, while the penthouse suites really take luxury and space to the next level.

Our sailing was rather empty — only 19 of the 54 suites were occupied — and we were upgraded to a higher suite category (I believe they had blocked most of the entry level room categories, as they were doing some minor updates to them ahead of the ship heading to the Caribbean). So let me share my thoughts on that suite first, and then I’ll share some pictures of other suites that I had the opportunity to tour as well.

We stayed in an Appartement Prestige, which is one of the more premium standard suite categories, but below the duplex suites and penthouse suites. These suites are marketed as being an average of 1,119 square feet (104 square meters), so they’re incredibly spacious.

We were assigned suite 518, located on the fifth floor. The hallways on the Corinthian are just stunning, as you can see below. It really feels more like a luxury hotel than a ship, especially in terms of the width of the hallway.

The concept of forgetting that one is on a ship continued inside the suite. The interior felt more to me like a “Palace” hotel in France, than what you’d expect at sea. I can’t even imagine how much money was spent on the interiors, as the quality of the finishes, from the wall treatments to the carpet, as well as the furniture, was just unreal.

Upon entering the suite, there was first a dining area with a table and a chair, as well as a desk with a chair (that chair could also be moved over to the dining table). It’s not often you get this kind of space in a cruise ship suite.

The minibar was also in this area, and was well stocked, with everything being complimentary. This included a Nespresso coffee machine, cocktails, wine, beer, soft drinks, etc. They were also happy to replenish the minibar however you wanted, so there are really no limits.

That entry area then flowed into the living room, which was gorgeous. It had a couch and a coffee table, as well as a hidden TV (which would pop up from in front of the mirror).

Waiting on the dining table was a lovely welcome amenity, consisting of some freshly baked treats, a fruit plate, and a bottle of Veuve Clicquot 2015 Rose. There was also an Orient Express branded journal, along with two Orient Express water bottles, which guests could take home.

Double doors then led into the bedroom, which had a very plush king size bed.

Much like with the bedroom, the bathroom will make you forget that you’re on a ship, as it had double sinks, a soaking tub, a walk-in shower with amazing water pressure, and a toilet in a separate room.

There were also a couple of closet areas, so there was plenty of space to store luggage and clothes.

The suite then had a balcony that stretched the entire length of the suite, with very comfortable furniture.

Beyond the generally beautiful design, it has to be pointed out just how over the top everything was. I mean, the deck furniture uses fabrics from Loro Piana, just to give you a sense of just how high-end it is.

Housekeeping in the room was great (it was taken care of twice daily, and always well timed), butler service was very useful (more on that a bit later, when I talk about service), Starlink Wi-Fi was lightning fast, and I also love how Orient Express Sailing Yachts includes laundry. You could get unlimited washing, dry cleaning, etc., so that’s a very nice feature.

In the interest of checking out different suite products, I also had the chance to tour the Suite Panoramique, which is the entry level accommodation onboard, located on levels four and five. These are 506 square feet (47 square meters), so they’re spacious for an entry level suite on a cruise.

This had the same general design concept as the suite we were in, except there wasn’t a fully separate living area. The suite had a comfortable king size bed, a desk with a chair, a dining table, and a huge window with a double daybed of sorts.

While there was no bathtub, the bathroom still had double sinks, a walk-in shower, and a toilet in a separate room.

To point out the obvious, these entry level suites don’t have balconies. Of course people prefer to have balconies, but this is just a simple reality of the difference between sailboats and cruise ships, in terms of how many levels there are, how far above water they are, etc.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ top end suites are really next level, so I also had the chance to tour the Zephyr Suite, which is located on level seven, and is the second most premium suite onboard. This two bedroom suite has 2,486 square feet (231 square meters) of interior space, plus a terrace that’s 1,206 square feet (112 square meters).

What I thought was so cool was how unique the design of this suite was, as the top suite products seem to have a totally original design. This very much had a residential vibe, with a long hallway connecting the various parts of the suite.

However, perhaps the coolest feature was the replica of an Orient Express Heritage cabin, intended to pay homage to the legendary train.

The Orient Express Sailing Yachts Corinthian has two pools onboard, with one being rather traditional, and one being unlike anything else at sea (at least to my knowledge). The main “leisure” pool is located on the fifth floor, at the back of the ship. While the pool has beautiful aesthetics and lovely deck space around it, this isn’t some destination pool in and of itself. So if a huge pool is a crucial factor in picking a ship, Four Seasons Yachts might be a better option.

We’re all different, and personally, I’m not much of a pool person. Quite to the contrary, I actually loved this pool deck, since it was mostly covered and in the shade, so I could nicely sit there and enjoy the breeze (funny enough, Four Seasons Yachts has an amazing pool, but I didn’t actually spend much time there, due to the lack of shade).

The ship then has a second pool, which is among the most memorable you’ll find on any ship. The lap pool is 54 feet (16 meters) long, and it’s located under the sails. It really feels like you’re in a cave, since it’s on a deck that’s one level down from the main upper deck. What a pool!

On the pool front, really my only disappointment was the lack of a hot tub. As much as I find hot tubs to be kind of gross, I do love them, especially on a ship, so I was sad there wasn’t one of those. In general, the newer ultra high end cruise lines seem to be lacking in that department (the same was true on Four Seasons Yachts).

Beyond the pool setup, on the seventh floor you’ll find a huge deck you can hang out on. There are lots of lounge chairs out here, though it’s not necessarily that popular for just lounging around. The star of the show here is what’s above.

The time when the deck really gets popular is when the ship pulls into or out of ports, given the panoramic views from up here, plus the ability to watch the sails be lowered and raised. I must say, it was absolutely mesmerizing to watch. They made a big event of departures, with live music, cocktails, etc. It really felt like a cocktail reception, only more intimate.

Speaking of deck space, another fun aspect of the ship is how you can actually just freely walk up to the deck in front of the bridge, and even all the way to the bow. How fun!

The Orient Express Sailing Yachts Corinthian wellness complex is located on the fourth floor, and that includes a Guerlain Spa. This area is an impressive 5,380 square feet (500 square meters), with four treatment suites (including a double suite), as well as all kinds of other traditional spa facilities.

Guests can always use the facilities, even without an appointment, and that includes a sauna, steam room, relaxation area, locker rooms, etc.

The spa treatment rooms are absolutely gorgeous, whether we’re talking about the couples room, or the individual ones.

Ford and I got a couples massage during our final day (where we were at sea), and I can honestly say it was one of the best spa treatments I’ve ever had. Not only was the therapist I had incredible, but the massage bed was so comfortable, and there was something so calming about the view, the gentle sway of the ship, etc.

For those curious about the pricing, you can find part of the spa menu below.

The ship also has a full hair salon and barber shop, so there are no shortage of opportunities to get your grooming needs taken care of here. The barber shop even leads to the speakeasy — more on that later.

The Orient Express Sailing Yachts Corinthian has a gym located on the fourth floor, which can be accessed by guests 24/7. The gym isn’t huge, but is more than sufficient given the size of the ship, in my opinion. Every time we used it, we were alone.

The gym had a good selection of cardio and weight equipment, as well as a separate room for aerobics, boxing, etc.

There was an excellent personal trainer onboard, and it was possible to schedule sessions with him at no extra cost. So it’s not just for group fitness, but even for personal sessions, on a space available basis. That’s really nice, as virtually any other cruise would charge for that, in my experience.

The Orient Express Sailing Yachts Corinthian has an incredibly impressive entertainment area, located on deck four. The issue is, it’s not really used a whole lot. Now, I’m not sure I’d actually call this an “issue,” but let me explain.

When you think of mega cruise ships, nightly shows and entertainment are among the most popular attractions. The thing is, the smaller the ship is, the less interest there is in things like this, and that’s especially true for the cruise lines that are primarily targeted at people who haven’t historically been cruisers.

So the Corinthian has a huge theater with dozens of seats, but there’s not a whole lot that goes on there.

Perhaps the more interesting entertainment feature is the private cinema, where you can have them screen a movie (or whatever) for you.

There’s even a recording studio onboard — what a cool concept, and in addition to being able to play instruments here, I heard people have used this to record podcasts, etc.

On the topic of entertainment, the ship also has a card room on the fourth floor, with chess, checkers, decks of cards, etc.

Separately, there’s also the yacht club, which is basically a very elegant lounge area where guests can hang out, watch TV, etc.

Lastly, the ship has the library on the fourth floor, which has an incredible selection of books. Everything on the Corinthian is so thoughtful, including the book selection. As it was explained to us, the 1,500-book library is supposed to represent the most important books of the century, and were curated by the historic Parisian bookshop Galignani.

I know there’s sometimes confusion about whether Orient Express Sailing Yachts is kids friendly, and the answer is… sort of.

On most voyages, guests onboard must be 16 years of age or older. However, on dedicated family voyages, children ages six months to 15 years old are allowed as well. Infants under six months aren’t permitted onboard, and per the terms, “families traveling with little ones under two years old must be accompanied by a dedicated babysitter throughout their voyage.”

Quite honestly, it’s logical that Orient Express Sailing Yachts would have this policy, since the ship’s venues feel really intimate, the pools aren’t huge, etc.

For family voyages, the Corinthian does have a kids club onboard, which offers activities with a dedicated team. Babysitting services can also be arranged for excursions or gala evenings. But in terms of being kids friendly, I definitely think it’s an area where Four Seasons Yachts wins, as all voyages are kids friendly, the pool is huge, and there’s both a kids club and teens club.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts has an incredibly impressive selection of restaurants, bars, and lounges onboard, with the culinary vision overseen by well-known chef Yannick Alléno. Before I get into details, let me just say that I found the quality of food and drinks onboard to be truly exceptional.

I try not to exaggerate, because I think far too many people are a little too generous when describing food on cruises (or flights, for that matter — what’s with all these people describing airplane food as Michelin dining?). However, I found the quality of catering on Orient Express Sailing Yachts to just be in a completely different league than Four Seasons Yachts.

I was also delighted by the generosity of the included options, with an incredible alcohol selection, caviar accompanying dishes at breakfast, lunch, and dinner (and even cocktails), etc. It’s also interesting to note that no reservations are allowed onboard, except at the fine dining restaurant that costs extra.

Everything was always available whenever we wanted it, though people will otherwise probably have mixed feelings on that policy (conversely, the issue when you do allow reservations is that people hog them and then just cancel at the last minute, leaving other guests with limited options).

Anyway, here are the most significant outlets onboard Orient Express Sailing Yachts:

With that out of the way, let’s get into the venues in a bit more detail.

La Terrasse is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ all-day dining restaurant, serving breakfast, lunch, and dinner. It’s located at the back of the sixth floor, and has both indoor and outdoor seating. The fact that this is the casual restaurant really tells you the quality of the experience, as there are white tablecloths all hours of the day.

This is the primary restaurant where breakfast is served, and you can find that menu below.

Breakfast is entirely a la carte, though at the start of the meal, a basket with a rotating selection of croissants and pastries was brought out.

There was a large selection of fresh juices and coffee available. My one disappointment was that the coffee was just okay, and clearly came from a machine. That’s ironic, because there’s plenty of delicious barista coffee on the ship, so this seems to be one of the only venues where that’s the case. Given the quality of service onboard, I’m sure they’d also be happy to get you a coffee from somewhere else, if you prefer.

We found the breakfast selection to be very good, and over the course of our stay tried the acai bowl with coconut and seasonal fruit, chia pudding with fresh mango, the mixed berry plate, the crispy and soft blinis with caviar cream and smoked salmon, the avocado toast, and more.

We also came to La Terrasse one day for lunch, and you can find that menu below.

We split the chickpea hummus with parmesan to start, and then had the smoked salmon club sandwich and Thai beef salad as our mains. At our server’s insistence, we finished off with a floating island for dessert. YUM.

We also had dinner here our first evening, and you can find that menu below.

To start, we had the smoked salmon with blinis and sour cream, and the gazpacho.

Then for mains, we had the pepper crusted beef fillet with cognac and cream sauce, and the red tuna teriyaki style, along with some sides.

Lastly, we finished off the meal with a selection from the cheese trolley, plus the vanilla millefeuille.

Across the board, the food and service were exceptional, so it’s amazing that this is just the most basic restaurant onboard, as it only gets better from there.

L’Ecrin is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ elevated dinner restaurant, with a focus on seafood and pasta. It’s located on the sixth floor, and it exclusively has indoor seating. This restaurant doesn’t cost extra, but in my opinion is on par with the paid restaurant on some of the other top ships.

We went here one evening for dinner, and you can find the menu below.

At the start of the meal, we were offered some sinfully delicious bread, along with some cured meats. I’ll talk more about service in a bit, but I might as well just mention in passing how good the crew was about our dietary preferences. For example, we mentioned when we boarded how we don’t eat pork, so without having to say anything, we were brought something that fit our needs.

We took an unusual approach to ordering. To start, we shared the seabass carpaccio with citrus marinade, and the spaghetti with caviar. My gosh, not only was the caviar portion on the spaghetti massive, but the overall flavor of the dish was incredible, as the beurre blanc combined with caviar had quite the unique flavor profile.

Then for mains, we had the warm lobster with olive oil and mayonnaise and the caponata and polenta. Again, this was very, very good.

For dessert, while I had heard amazing things about the suzette pasta (flambeed tableside), we decided on the signature bronte pistachio ice cream coupe, which was insanely indulgent.

What a meal! This was definitely my favorite restaurant onboard.

La Table by Yannick Alléno is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ most premium dinner restaurant, and it’s the only venue that comes at an extra charge, at the rate of €400 per person for the tasting menu.

First, we have to talk about the restaurant as such. Can you believe this is on a ship? This is without a doubt the most beautiful dining venue I’ve ever seen on a ship. With just over half a dozen tables, it’s also a really intimate space.

The tasting menu is constantly changing, and you can find the menu for our dinner below.

I’ll let the pictures speak for themselves…

The meal was very good, with service that matched the food quality. It really felt like a Michelin-starred dining experience in terms of the presentation, the service flow, etc.

While this was excellent, I will say, I wouldn’t necessarily feel compelled to dine here again. That’s just because the standard restaurants are so great that I don’t necessarily think it’s worth the incremental cost. At a minimum, don’t feel like you’re missing out if you don’t eat here… but definitely do take a look at the restaurant, to appreciate its beauty!

L’Encre is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ venue that’s exclusively open for lunch, and it was definitely my favorite lunch spot onboard. It’s basically a circular counter with a little over a dozen seats, so the setting is stunning.

You can find the menu below. Think of the concept as basically being like a seafood omakase, where they just keep bringing you out more dishes. Of course you can customize however you want, ask for more of whatever you really like, skip dishes, etc. Below is a sampling of what we ate.

La Piscine Lounge is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ poolside venue, serving drinks, snacks, and even full meals, throughout most of the day. It’s even opening at night, and can double as a bar for a pre-dinner drink. It’s a beautiful space, definitely not your typical pool bar!

You can find the drink list and menu for that below.

We had an afternoon snack here one day, and split the mezze and the veggie burger, both of which were very good.

Le Bar de la Bibliotheque is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ coffee shop in the library area, and it’s a lovely place from which to get some work done, read a book, etc.

Here you’ll find barista coffee, homemade cakes, fresh juices, kombucha, and more.

Le Wagon Bar is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ primary bar venue, and it’s only open late at night. It’s intended to be a replica of the circular bar found on the modern Orient Express trains, with 1920s and 1930s heritage craftsmanship, so it’s a very cool space.

There’s a DJ there at night. The one thing to be aware of is that it only opens really late (9:30PM at the earliest, but often 10PM), and if you’re on a quieter sailing, there might not be too much of a vibe here. However, I’ve heard that on other sailings this place can be packed — it’s all about the crowd on a particular cruise.

I ordered the signature Corinthian Martini, with gin, vodka, champagne cordial, and — naturally, like everything on this ship — caviar!

Next, Le Speakeasy Bar is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ speakeasy. The idea is basically that people do a bar crawl, and it’s common to move between both bars in the same evening. Much like Le Wagon Bar, this one also opens really late.

The bar is located through a hidden door in the barbershop, so they’re really committed to that speakeasy theme.

This bar even has a separate smoking room, which I’m sure smokers will appreciate (as it’s the only indoor space on the ship where you can smoke).

This bar also has some unique signature cocktails, and you can find that drink list below.

While not included, they are very proud of their liquor selection here, with some bottles that are older than my dad (and at a cost of up to $2,400 per shot — yowzers!).

Tempted as I was, I stuck to one of the included martinis. 😉

Le Flybridge Bar is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ outdoor bar space located on the top floor. While this is open quite frequently, it really only gets busy when the ship sets sail, given the interest in watching the sails in action.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts of course has 24/7 room service, which is included, with no additional costs. The standard room service menu is on the basic side, but service very much falls into the category of them wanting to make guests happy, so they’re also happy to get you something from any restaurant, if you’d like (but since the menus are always changing, they’re not published in the room service menu).

We did have room service dinner one evening…

…and the final morning we had breakfast in our suite as well (we accidentally ordered too much).

Our amazing butler, Reuben, also gladly brought us cappuccinos and protein shakes, so they were happy to accommodate guests however they could.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts has a very impressive included drink menu. You can find the standard alcoholic drink list below, though some venues have additional options or signature cocktails customized to that venue.

Having Veuve Clicquot La Grande Dame 2018 as the house champagne is very impressive. And let me just say, they’re also not cheap with the pours — you can barely go anywhere without having a glass pushed on you. 😉

Of course there’s also a premium drink list with even more special wines and spirits, and those come at an extra cost.

I have to acknowledge that our sailing was rather empty, so the staff to guest ratio on this sailing was unreal. That being said, it wasn’t just the ratio that was amazing, but the quality of staff was really incredible as well. If you don’t have good staff, they’ll find a way to disappoint even if the staff to guest ratio is amazing.

I’m not exaggerating when I say that service on Orient Express Sailing Yachts was flawless in terms of attention to detail, and that was such a contrast to our Four Seasons Yachts experience.

It’s hard to even pinpoint any one area that impressed me, because it was just very consistent, polished, and proactive, across the board. Let me just give a few examples:

As I said in my Four Seasons Yachts review, while we had an amazing time, we had way more service issues than I’d consider to be acceptable, given the price point. This was exactly the opposite, and it was just flawless service experience after flawless service experience. So while I’m sure service is consistently good, I’m sure the empty sailing also contributed to taking this to the next level.

We were definitely on an odd sailing, in terms of seasonality, since we were on the second to last voyage before the ship sailed across the Atlantic, to start the winter season in the Caribbean.

Our sailing was empty, with just 19 of the 54 suites occupied, so there were fewer than 40 guests. It really felt like having a private yacht, as we rarely saw others, and we’d go to restaurants for dinner, at most a handful of other tables would be occupied.

On our sailing, almost everyone seemed to be a European retiree, so it was maybe in line with what you’d expect from the stereotypical guest profile of Orient Express trains. However, Ford has had some clients on Orient Express Sailing Yachts, and based on the feedback he has gotten, the ship can be an absolute scene, with some pretty over-the-top people.

The guest profile that Orient Express Sailing Yachts gets is probably a bit different than almost any other cruise line. For one, the ship has already been chartered multiple times in its first season, so you can imagine the kinds of people we’re talking about. And even on sailings that haven’t been chartered, there have been some A-list people onboard.

So anyway, we had a very pleasant, understated crowd onboard, but I’ve also heard the crowd can make for quite some people watching, especially for sailings in the South of France, etc.

As I said at the beginning, my goal here is to be as objective as possible, so what feedback do I have? Honestly, as much as I have a critical eye, I think there are shockingly few areas for improvements. Here are the things that stood out to me:

I also want to acknowledge that Trek Trendy had published a review of the Orient Express Corinthian, and I think that’s worth watching for a different perspective. I think he was being totally fair with some of his critique, but I had a different experience:

I travel a ton, and as much as I have so many amazing experiences, I’m almost always excited to go home, given that I miss family, and travel is sort of my “job.” I have to be honest, the Orient Express Corinthian was the first time in recent memory where I thought to myself “man, I wish it weren’t over.”

Earlier this year I experienced Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection and Four Seasons Yachts, and they’re both great in their own ways. However, Orient Express Sailing Yachts is really in a different league. Yes, it’s priced at the top end of the market, but it also includes the most, and I really appreciate that. There’s something nice about paying a high voyage cost in advance, but then feeling like everything is included.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts really is an unbelievable product, from the design of the ship, to the incredible restaurant and bar concepts, to the service. If you can swing it — and especially if you’ve never taken a cruise before — I can’t recommend this enough.

What’s your take on the Orient Express cruise concept?

So a 4 day cruise for 2 with terrace is 29k EUR in May 2027... aside from the price, looks amazing.

It’s funny that a lot of the highlights of the room etc are that “you forget you are on a ship”. What is the point of this over being in a nice hotel in a nice city. Especially if you only visit and disembark in one city?

Just to clarify, as I’ve heard this mentioned in other reviews as well, the deck furniture is by the Italian company EXTETA, only the fabric used is from Loro Piana Interiors. Loro Piana does not manufacture furniture.

Kudos on the Odyssey of a review! Like others, I'm thrilled you are providing more cruise comparisons for your previous reviews on RC and Four Seasons. Looking forward to reading about your non-hotel-affiliated cruise experiences. I've been a reader for years and appreciate the lack of BS. This is BS: "I have no incentive to be anything other than honest." That would only be true if your husband couldn't earn a commission from booking readers on the cruise line. But that's not the case, as you link in the previous paragraph. And of course, the only reason you took the cruise is because your husband can earn a commission booking these trips. Fair enough, just don't pretend you don't have an incentive to give a positive review here. It's the same reason why you can and do write very critical (and witty!) airline reviews (Ford doesn't earn a commission from booking TunisAir and earns almost no commission if any from any airline). But we'll never see the same level of candor on any product Ford can book. Especially one where the experience was comped or discounted (will hotels and cruise lines continue comping Ford and letting him bring his blogger husband if blogger husband writes honest negative reviews?). Again, great review, I appreciate the attempt at disclosing and minimizing conflicts of interest, but it's dishonest to say you have no incentive to be anything other than honest.

So no Tunisair review after all — boo! Then again, being downgraded from J is already a big bummer, so perhaps that article on the downgrade is supposed to suffice? Too bad we’re not going to get any views of Tunis or Marseille… Anyway, that aside: I truly appreciate your commitment to review luxury cruises at this level. My word, the amount of commitment you’ve put into this review is just as much as Orient Express puts into its entire experience. You’ll pay top dollar, about as much as a couple of Air France La Première flights, but you’ll remember those tens of thousands of dollars spent as among the best you’ve ever spent. So yes: being able to swing it at the age of 35-ish is already a dream come true, the sort of thing that retirees splurge on after having saved all their lives. To be able to experience the cruises of Four Seasons, Ritz-Carlton and now Orient Express, all within a year’s span — and this after not having cruised since childhood — is astounding. Perhaps you should launch a spinoff blog, One Cruise at a Time (OCAAT)? ;)
