#6071. United Airlines' Rare Arctic Flights Only 46% Full: Here's Why

United Airlines' ambitious expansion into Greenland has yet to deliver strong passenger numbers. The carrier launched nonstop flights between Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) and Nuuk International Airport (GOH) in June of last year, establishing a unique link between the United States and Greenland. However, in its second summer of operations, load factors deteriorated further, with more than half of its available seats going empty.

The opening of Nuuk's new international airport in November 2024 was intended to transform Greenland's accessibility and stimulate tourism growth. However, inadequate tourism infrastructure, high vacation costs, and a relatively small underlying travel market are among the factors that appear to be limiting demand for United's flights.

According to the US Department of Transportation's T-100 data, United transported 3,709 passengers across 48 flights between Newark and Nuuk from June through August. Passenger numbers declined by 5.2% year-over-year despite an 11.6% capacity increase. Consequently, its 166-seat Boeing 737 MAX 8s averaged just 77 passengers per flight, achieving a load factor of 46.5%.

The figures are particularly concerning when compared with United's broader transatlantic network. Nuuk recorded the lowest load factor by a considerable margin, trailing the service from Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) to Reykjavík's Keflavik International Airport (KEF) by more than 20 percentage points. Even United's other new European destinations, including Glasgow and Santiago de Compostela, performed substantially better during their first summer.

United commenced its second season a week earlier, increasing June capacity by 50% despite passenger numbers declining by 6.1%. This resulted in a particularly poor 32.8% load factor across the month. However, the challenges extend beyond United's scheduling decisions, with Greenland Airports recently acknowledging that insufficient accommodation is constraining aviation growth.

“Revenue from air traffic is expected to be lower than originally projected, partly because hotel capacity in both Nuuk and Ilulissat continues to be a limiting factor.”

While Greenland has invested heavily in its aviation infrastructure with its new $300 million airport, its hospitality industry has struggled to keep pace. A 2024 capacity analysis commissioned by Visit Greenland identified just 1,039 available beds across hotels, apartments, and hostels in and around Nuuk. National carrier Air Greenland has also identified accommodation shortages as a significant constraint on further passenger growth.

Affordability represents another major obstacle. Visit Greenland's 2023 study of Greenland's prospective tourism markets found that 35% of potential North American visitors considered Greenland too expensive. Unlike neighboring Iceland, Greenland has no intercity road network, leaving tourists dependent on relatively expensive domestic flights and boat journeys to explore the country.

Greenland's small population also means that United cannot rely on the ongoing business and visiting-friends-and-relatives traffic that supports many of its European services. Furthermore, Greenland has an established cruise tourism industry, meaning that growing visitor numbers do not automatically translate into additional demand for scheduled international flights.

United's island operations often differ significantly on the ground from its regional operations on the US mainland, making it an adventure in itself.

United's twice-weekly schedule also limits itinerary flexibility, particularly given Greenland's susceptibility to weather-related flight disruptions. Despite requiring a connection, Icelandair's Greenland network offers more frequent service and access to four destinations, potentially providing a more attractive alternative for travelers who want to explore beyond Nuuk or combine Greenland and Iceland in a single vacation.

Geopolitical uncertainty may also have contributed to weaker demand in 2026. President Donald Trump's ambitions to acquire Greenland generated considerable international attention during the important early-year booking period. However, while some tour operators reported declining bookings, others experienced increased interest, making it difficult to establish whether the political situation adversely affected United's flights.

Bookings down 20%, but a subsequent increase in inquiries

Increased interest from US, UK and German travelers

The recent openings of international airports at Qaqortoq and Ilulissat should support Greenland's longer-term tourism ambitions. However, from January 1, 2027, Greenland Airports is more than doubling its summer international passenger fee to DKK 1,182 ($171), further challenging affordability. Ironically, the justification for the increase is that revenue has come in lower than projected, “partly because hotel capacity in both Nuuk and Ilulissat continues to be a limiting factor.”

The reality is that United has solved the challenge of getting Americans to Greenland, but Greenland has not yet solved the challenges of accommodating them, transporting them around the island, and making their vacations affordable. So while United's Greenland services remain scheduled for 2027, achieving sustainable performance will require considerable effort to stimulate stronger demand or adjustments to fare structures and capacity.

#6070. Norse Atlantic On Brink Of Collapse, Admits “Financial Situation Is Critical”

Back in August 2026, all-Boeing 787 airline Norse Atlantic Airways announced it was in a rough financial spot, and was pursuing a sale, merger, or other arrangement. Not a whole lot of solutions have been found since then, and it seems like things have only gotten worse. The airline has just revealed the latest regarding its financial situation, and it’s not looking good.

Norse Atlantic has today provided an update on its financial situation and ongoing strategic review. There’s no point in paraphrasing this, so here’s the direct statement from the airline:

The Company’s financial situation is critical. It is dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs and to continue its operations. Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover. In parallel, the Board and management have diligently considered other available options, including ACMI contracts. Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution.

To state the obvious, this sounds really, really bad. When the company is publicly stating that its “financial situation is critical” and that it needs to secure financing to meet “short-term liquidity needs,” you know things aren’t good. So we’ll see what comes of this, but it seems like there’s a very real chance the airline could simply liquidate in the coming weeks.

The airline industry can be a funny business, and there’s no clearer example of that than Norse Atlantic Airways. The airline launched in 2022, with the goal of operating long haul, low cost flights, particularly across the Atlantic.

That wasn’t exactly a unique business model, because this was exactly what Norwegian did, before it discontinued long haul flights in 2021. Not only was the idea sort of copied, but Norse Atlantic had some executives from Norwegian, and even picked up the planes that Norwegian previously flew.

But as is all too common in the airline industry, clearly they thought it would be different this time around… it wasn’t. So in 2024 we saw the airline update its business model, making the focus less about operating regularly scheduled commercial flights, and more about leasing out aircraft, all while reducing its fleet.

The company got a lifeline when IndiGo decided to lease some Norse Atlantic 787s to dabble in long haul flying, ahead of the airline taking delivery of its own Airbus A350s. However, between all the airspace closures, high oil costs, and generally declining performance at IndiGo as the airline increasingly moved away from its core strengths, the airline recently decided to scrap that experiment, and stop leasing planes from Norse Atlantic.

Since then, opportunities for Norse Atlantic have been limited. The airline did manage to lease a couple of Dreamliners to the “new” Pakistan International Airlines, but for an airline with 12 planes, that hardly pays the bills.

Norse Atlantic does still operate some of its own flights, but in a very limited capacity. The airline has some flights from Europe to Thailand and the United States, but most are seasonal, and they’re a fraction of what they previously were.

Really there’s just one idea that comes to mind for me — we know that Southwest Airlines wants to start long haul flights. The airline had been considering a Boeing 787 order, and was possibly even looking at ways to get planes faster than from a direct order (which requires waiting for years).

Could these dozen Norse Atlantic 787s somehow end up at Southwest? The interiors would just need some updates (assuming the airline wants to offer business class), but talk about a quick way to grow a decent sized fleet.

Norse Atlantic has released a statement admitting that its “financial situation is critical,” and that the company’s future is “dependent on securing financing to meet short-term liquidity needs.”

Financial issues at the company started when… well, it launched. Norse Atlantic was just a direct replica of Norwegian, which had failed. When the airline realized that the long haul, low cost business model doesn’t really work, they tried to pivot to wet leasing. And while there’s some demand for that, it’s also not a 100% consistent business in terms of demand.

The tone of this announcement sure is serious, so I’m curious to see how this evolves. I feel bad for the frontline employees at the airline, of course, as they’re the victims in this.

What do you make of Norse Atlantic’s “critical” financial situation?

#6068. Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi

President Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

“As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”

Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., said part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

“They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” said Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

“I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump said Monday. “I think he's backing down.”

Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a big reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”

“I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”

During remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

“Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat said, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

“Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”

But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

He stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”

Trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the company’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

The administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”

Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”

“Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear issues dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”

#6067. Marriott Bonvoy Elite Status Soft Landings For 2027: Drop Only One Tier

Marriott Bonvoy has just revealed its status soft landing policy for the next membership year, and it’s good news (well, at least for those who don’t requalify for their current status tier).

Marriott Bonvoy has just revealed its status soft landing policy for the 2027 status year, for situations where someone doesn’t qualify for a particular elite tier based on their activity in 2026. Specifically, elite members who don’t achieve the published criteria to maintain their status will only drop down at most one elite tier.

In other words, Ambassador Elites will at most drop to Titanium Elite, Titanium Elites will at most drop to Platinum Elite, Platinum Elites will at most drop to Gold Elite, and Gold Elites will drop at most to Silver Elite.

For what it’s worth, this policy matches Marriott’s historical approach to status soft landings. Before Marriott and Starwood merged, back when Marriott’s loyalty program was named Marriott Rewards, Marriott consistently had a status soft landing policy. With this, Marriott Rewards members never dropped more than one elite tier per year, regardless of their activity.

That policy has continued since the new program was formed, including for the next year. However, there’s no guarantee this will continue to be the policy in the future. For those curious, the status offered as part of the soft landing also does count toward lifetime elite status. So if you’re downgraded from Titanium to Platinum based on a soft landing, that year of Platinum will add to your total.

During the pandemic, we saw airline and hotel loyalty programs largely extend elite status several times. This made sense, given the extent to which business travel decreased for many. However, with the huge increase in leisure travel and all the new ways to earn elite status, we’ve seen elite ranks swell.

Personally I think the concept of a status soft landing makes a lot of sense. After all, sometimes life conditions change for people, and in many cases those changes are just temporary. If you drop from top tier status to no status, you don’t really have much of an incentive to stay loyal to that hotel group when your travel picks up again.

By offering a soft landing, loyalty programs can try to build more of a long term relationship with members, and that’s a positive. We also see some programs allow members to pause their status for a year or extend status as a one-time exception based on life circumstances, and I think that’s a great policy as well.

Marriott Bonvoy has a generous status soft landing policy for 2027, for those who don’t requalify for status in 2026. If you didn’t requalify for your current status tier with Marriott Bonvoy in 2026, you can expect that you’ll be downgraded at most one status level.

What do you make of Marriott Bonvoy’s soft landing policy for status?

#6065. Why Southwest Airlines Likely Won't Fly The Boeing 737 MAX 8-200 Like Allegiant Air & Ryanair

Southwest Airlines has not publicly issued a formal explanation for why it does not operate the 737 MAX 8-200, but its commercial direction in 2026 points straight toward the underlying reason. The 8-200 is engineered to pack maximum seating density into a single-aisle cabin, whereas Southwest has spent 2026 reshaping its cabin experience around assigned seating, extra-legroom rows, new fare tiers, and upcoming Icon lounges. If an airline moves away from open-seating boarding toward structured comfort and paid upgrades, squeezing 15 to 20 extra seats onto every aircraft works directly against that strategy.

Contrasting Southwest against ultra-low-cost operators such as Ryanair and Allegiant Air shows how the same Boeing 737 MAX family can serve massively different commercial models. Ryanair configures its 8-200 jets for maximum seat count, Allegiant pairs high-capacity seating with extra-legroom rows, and Southwest keeps 175 seats across its standard 737 MAX 8 and 737-800 aircraft. The way in which the 8-200 is designed, how carriers like Ryanair and Allegiant use it, and how Southwest's 2026 product shift unfolds explains why the Dallas-based carrier is unlikely to chase maximum-density narrowbody layouts.

The 737 MAX 8-200 is a high-density derivative of the standard 737 MAX 8 created to help ultra-low-cost operators push seat counts on single-aisle routes. As One Mile At A Time notes, the variant keeps the same fuselage length, overall airframe dimensions, engines, maximum takeoff weight, and range capability as a baseline 737 MAX 8. Contrary to a standard stretching of the airframe or altering core flight performance, Boeing focused on regulatory evacuation thresholds and interior floor-space efficiency so airlines could carry more passengers per flight.

For the allowance of higher passenger loads while meeting evacuation rules, Boeing added an extra pair of emergency exit doors behind the wing on the 737 MAX 8-200. Reporting from Aviation Week explains that this mid-cabin exit modification raised the design capacity from the standard 737 MAX 8 ceiling up to 200 seats initially, with later configurations reaching up to 210 seats. Across Europe, aviation rules cap the 737 MAX 8-200 at 202 passengers, forming a strict ceiling even in high-demand short-haul markets.

Achieving those higher seat totals comes from the design of the high-density 8-200 configuration rather than any single airline's livery or onboard branding. As highlighted in Simple Flying analysis, packing additional rows into a single-aisle cabin of roughly 11 feet 7 inches (approximately 3.53 meters) in width means using slimline seats, tighter seat pitch, compact lavatories, and reduced galley space. Those hardware and floorplan choices lower cost per seat on paper, but they leave far less room for cabin comfort or generous legroom.

Ryanair is the clearest real-world example of the 737 MAX 8-200 deployed strictly as a high-density, low-fare machine across busy short-haul European routes. As shown in trip reports from WillAviation, Ryanair fits 197 slimline seats spaced at 28 inches (approximately 71.1 centimeters) of pitch, the distance from one seat back to the next, compared with 189 seats on its older 737-800 aircraft. Adding eight extra seats per jet spreads fixed operating costs across more fare-paying flyers on high-frequency point-to-point sectors.

Squeezing 197 seats into that single-aisle cabin, Ryanair leans on interior space compromises tailored to ultra-low-cost operations. The layout relies on three small lavatories and removes some galley space, trading onboard amenity space and restroom capacity for lower cost per seat, as noted by Simple Flying. On short European flights built around rock-bottom base fares and rapid turnarounds, maximizing seat count per departure takes clear priority over extra cabin room.

As the 737 MAX 8-200's main operator by a wide margin, Ryanair shows how directly the variant supports an ultra-low-cost business model. Packing 197 seats into the airframe helps lower per-seat costs across high-frequency schedules, so that Ryanair does not have to step up to a larger aircraft type and change its single-type business model.

The MAX 8-200 is a special edition of the MAX 8 developed for ultra-low-cost carriers that seek to maximize the workhorse's seating capacity.

Allegiant Air takes a slightly more segmented approach to the 737 MAX 8-200, combining high overall passenger capacity with a dedicated block of extra-legroom seats aimed at leisure travelers. As One Mile At A Time reports, Allegiant configures its 737 MAX 8-200 aircraft with 190 seats, including 21 extra-legroom Allegiant Extra seats. That cabin arrangement allows flyers who want extra space to pay a little extra for it but keep the total seat count substantially higher than a standard narrowbody layout.

For a leisure-focused airline whose routes center on vacation and seasonal demand, having high-capacity rows and paid legroom upgrades has a clear commercial role. Reporting from One Mile At A Time notes that Allegiant Extra seating provides at least six inches (approximately 15.2 centimeters) of extra pitch over standard rows, paired with power ports and larger overhead bins. Even with those extra-legroom seats built into the cabin, the 190-seat total remains a high-density narrowbody setup.

Comparing Allegiant's 190-seat layout against Ryanair's 197-seat configuration shows how airlines adapt the same 737 MAX 8-200 airframe to different revenue strategies. Both carriers take advantage of the 8-200's high-density capability to boost passenger volume per flight, but Allegiant sets aside 21 seats for extra-legroom upsells, not chasing the highest possible seat count across every row. Even with that nuance, Allegiant's leisure-driven density sits well apart from Southwest's evolving cabin model.

Southwest Airlines moves in the opposite direction from maximum-density narrowbody layouts, offering 175 seats on its standard 737 MAX 8 and 737-800 aircraft. As reported by Travel Weekly, Southwest has reconfigured jets to sell extra-legroom seats with 34 to 36 inches (approximately 86.4 to 91.4 centimeters) of pitch up front, while keeping standard seats at 31 inches (approximately 78.7 centimeters). That standard seat pitch already gives flyers roughly one inch (approximately 2.5 centimeters) more legroom than many flights on American, Delta, and United.

Squeezing 15 to 20 additional seats onto a Southwest 737, the jump from 175 seats into the 190-to-197-seat range seen on high-density layouts, would clash directly with that seating structure. Tighter row spacing or trimmed cabin spaces would take away the comfort edge Southwest is building across its extra-legroom rows and standard seats throughout the main cabin. Adding extra seats simply to chase peak density would undermine the legroom differentiation meant to win over higher-yielding domestic travelers.

Those cabin geometry trade-offs carry real weight for an airline that spent decades operating uniform single-class cabins with fast turns. Integrating 34-to-36-inch (approximately 86.4-to-91.4-centimeter) extra-legroom pitch and 31-inch (approximately 78.7-centimeter) standard pitch in a way that does not massively affect overall seat count is what shapes cabin layout, passenger comfort, and fare revenue across every flight. Keeping a 175-seat setup protects the legroom and seat segmentation Southwest now relies on across its fleet.

Ryanair is notable for asking Boeing to build a specific MAX 8 variant for high-density seating, while others configure A350s ten-abreast.

Southwest Airlines' recent cabin evolution has stemmed from a repositioning away from its old no-frills open-seating identity toward structured choices and elevated customer touchpoints. Highlighted in Simple Flying coverage, initiatives such as assigned seating, extra legroom rows, new premium fare types, and upcoming Icon lounges signal an airline reshaping how travelers experience the brand across its network. In that context, an ultra-dense narrowbody cabin designed around bare-bones squeezing projects the wrong brand message.

Customer perception and onboard atmosphere matter just as much as seat counts when an airline is actively rebranding its travel experience. Moving from open boarding to assigned seats and tiered fare options changes what flyers expect from the moment they book through boarding and lounge access. A cabin geared toward maximum crowding conflicts with a brand leaning into comfort, structure, and hospitality across every stage of the journey.

That brand shift mirrors a wider divide across commercial aviation between ultra-low-cost carriers pushing maximum density and airlines moving toward more space and premium options. Ryanair, Allegiant, VietJet, and Akasa Air have all committed to the 737 MAX 8-200, while airlines such as Southwest and United favor the standard 737 MAX 8 with fewer seats. Together, those opposing camps show why Southwest's brand direction ultimately points away from the 8-200.

Taken together, the 737 MAX 8-200 illustrates how a single airframe family can pull in opposite commercial directions depending on how an airline values seat volume versus cabin space. While the 8-200 gives ultra-low-cost and high-density operators extra exit capacity to push seat counts up to 197 or 190, Southwest Airlines has moved away from maximum squeezing toward assigned seating, extra-legroom rows, new premium fare tiers, and upcoming Icon lounges. Holding on to 175 seats on its standard 737 MAX 8 and 737-800 aircraft aligns naturally with that space-led shift, whereas packing 15 to 20 extra seats onto each jet would undermine the comfort edge Southwest is building.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Ultimately, Southwest does not need to publicly explain away the 737 MAX 8-200 for its fleet logic to come into sharp focus for travelers and industry watchers across the market. A high-density variant engineered to maximize seat count per departure simply does not match an airline repositioning around extra space, structured seating, and higher-tier customer touchpoints. Unless Southwest reverses course and abandons that 2026 product direction in favor of ultra-low-cost crowding across its single-aisle fleet, the 737 MAX 8-200 is unlikely to find a place in its aircraft lineup.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

More people are now willing to pay for extra legroom.

#6064. Chase Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card Review: Are The Benefits Worth The Fee?

The Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card is one of the most compelling co-branded airline credit cards out there. I’m a huge fan of the Air Canada Aeroplan program — even if you have no connection to Air Canada or Aeroplan, the program is fantastic for partner redemptions, and this card is worth being aware of. And if you do fly Air Canada with any frequency, the perks for travel on the airline are strong.

So this post is my in-depth Air Canada Aeroplan Card review. Let’s go over all the details, and discuss if the card is worth it.

Link: Learn more about the Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card

Before I review the Air Canada Aeroplan Card benefits in detail, here’s a high-level look at everything you need to know about the card:

Here are my thoughts on the Air Canada Aeroplan Card’s biggest pros and cons:

If you’re thinking about applying for the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card, you’re probably most interested in the welcome bonus it’s currently offering, along with its annual fee and general eligibility rules for getting the card. So let’s get into those details.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card currently has the following welcome bonus: Limited Time Offer: Earn up to 80,000 bonus points. Earn 60,000 bonus points after you spend $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months your account is open. Plus, up to 20,000 more bonus points by earning 50% more bonus points per $1 spent on purchases that normally earn 1 bonus point in the first 2 months from account opening..

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Aeroplan points to be worth 1.4 cents each. That means the 80,000 points are worth $1,120 to me. However, even if you have a different valuation of these points than I do, you can at least use the “Pay Yourself Back” feature to redeem these points for 1.25 cents each toward a travel purchase, so that’s a pretty high “cash out” value.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card is issued by Chase, and has pretty standard application restrictions:

While Chase doesn’t have a public credit score requirement for the Air Canada Aeroplan Card, you’ll have the best chances of approval if your score is in the good range or higher. That roughly translates to a minimum score of 670. However, people have been approved with lower scores and rejected with higher scores, as it’s one of only many factors that determine card eligibility.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card has a $195 annual fee. There’s no cost to add authorized users to the card, and their spending will count toward your points balance and any spending thresholds.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s a great card to use globally, and possibly even earn bonus rewards on your spending depending on what you’re using the card for.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Card has a well rounded rewards structure, among the most interesting you’ll find on any airline credit cards. This isn’t just about the number of points that you earn, but also about the additional rewards for spending. Specifically, the Aeroplan Card offers the following:

Those are some excellent bonus categories. For what it’s worth, the card offers 1x Aeroplan points on all other purchases, so there are better cards for everyday spending.

There’s a lot to love about Air Canada Aeroplan points, even if you don’t usually fly Air Canada or travel to Canada. Among other things:

I redeem miles through Aeroplan all the time, and consistently get great value. Booking award flights on Air Canada itself rather than other partners isn’t always the best deal, though, especially if you’re booking during a peak travel time, since Air Canada awards use dynamic pricing.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Card gives cardmembers plenty of opportunities to earn elite status with Air Canada Aeroplan. You get some status outright just for being a cardmember, and you can earn further status with spending.

Those who are approved for the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card receive Aeroplan 25K status. This is valid for as long as your account is open. Aeroplan Elite 25K is Air Canada’s entry level status, and includes travel perks with Air Canada, including:

Each year, those with the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card also receive 5,000 Status Qualifying Credits (SQCs) to help work toward the next level of Aeroplan status. This is automatic, but as I’ll cover below, you can stack additional credits on top through hitting certain spending thresholds in the calendar year.

For those curious, below are the Aeroplan elite requirements.

Beyond the automatic 5,000 SQCs you’ll receive each calendar year just for having the Air Canada Aeroplan Card, you can earn up to 20,000 additional credits by hitting spending thresholds. Here’s how that breaks down:

So you can earn a total of 25,000 SQCs each calendar year through the Air Canada Aeroplan Card.

Whether or not that’s worth it really depends on how much you fly Air Canada, and what the opportunity cost of your credit card spending is.

Those with the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card can get a one-tier status upgrade to Aeroplan 35K status when they spend $75,000 on the card in a calendar year. You’ll get status for the remainder of the calendar year you qualify and the entire following calendar year.

If you ask me, the value here is really for someone who is actually loyal to Air Canada. Aeroplan 35K status gets you three complimentary checked bags on Air Canada flights (vs. just one with Aeroplan 25K), 10 eUpgrade credits, and a 3x elite points multiplier on eligible Air Canada or Star Alliance flight bookings, among other things.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers a variety of valuable benefits and credits, beyond the elite status perks covered above. Some of these benefits are offered just for being a cardmember, while others can be earned with spending. The perks are pretty comprehensive, and you’ll find almost everything you could want short of lounge access. So let’s go over those.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers up to $100 in Air Canada statement credits when you make qualifying Air Canada purchases. The credits apply to paid airfare, taxes and fees on award flights, and inflight food and drinks, though onboard Wi-Fi is excluded.

This breaks down as two credits of up to $50 each, one from January 1 through June 30 and one from July 1 through December 31. If you book cash fares on Air Canada twice a year, this is an easy way to put $100 back in your pocket, and this benefit alone can cover about half of the card’s annual fee.

As an Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card holder, you can receive a 15% discount on the Aeroplan points required to book an award flight on Air Canada, Air Canada Express, or Air Canada Rouge. In practice, this also seems to work on partner award flights, as long as at least one segment is on Air Canada. The upside here can be absolutely huge, and it’s a great reason to have this card.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers a free first checked bag on Air Canada flights for the primary cardmember and up to eight others traveling on the same itinerary. This applies to itineraries with Air Canada, Air Canada Rouge, or Air Canada Express. The value of that could add up pretty quickly. There’s no need to actually pay for the ticket with the card, as long as you’re the primary cardmember and have your Aeroplan number linked to the reservation.

Once every four years, the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers a credit that’s valid toward a membership with Global Entry, TSA PreCheck, or NEXUS, worth up to $120. These are all programs that can save travelers time at the airport, and potentially even at the border.

I specifically love that the card also offers a NEXUS credit, since that’s historically something we haven’t seen card issuers offer. NEXUS is arguably the best of the three programs, since it gets you access to Global Entry, TSA PreCheck, and expedited immigration in Canada.

Admittedly this is probably more interesting in theory than in practice, but I still like where Aeroplan is going with this. Those with the Air Canada Aeroplan Card will automatically have carbon offsets purchased for their flights when redeeming Aeroplan points for an Air Canada flight.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card is a World Elite Mastercard, which comes with certain perks, including a concierge service and presale tickets for eligible events.

While you’ll want to consult the cardmember agreement for full details, the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers a variety of travel protection when paying with the card, including the following:

There’s another feature that you’ll find on the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card, which isn’t available on any other airline card. Specifically, the Aeroplan Credit Card offers a Pay Yourself Back feature, whereby cardmembers can apply their Aeroplan points toward travel purchases on any airline, hotel, or rental car, at the rate of 1.25 cents per point, up to 200,000 points per year.

This is an incredibly innovative concept, and something that cardmembers may find to be valuable. So whether you want to redeem your points for a stay at a Four Seasons or a flight on JetBlue, the possibilities are endless. It’s also a reason to potentially think of the welcome bonus differently — the bonus points earned with the welcome offer can over time be redeemed toward any recent purchase or even toward the card’s annual fee.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card also offers the ability to earn priority reward vouchers. Each can be used to get 50% off an eligible Aeroplan award ticket, and is valid for travel on Air Canada or a partner airline.

You earn these vouchers at the following four annual spending thresholds:

These can each be used in the same way, and the value depends on your status:

As you can tell, the value here will depend on your status and travel patterns, but there’s potentially quite a bit of value to be had.

While this is something that most people won’t be able to achieve, I love the concept behind this, and for some it might just be the best deal in travel. The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers what I’d consider to be the world’s most valuable companion certificate, for those who spend a million dollars per year on the card.

If you reach that threshold, you’ll receive an award redemption companion voucher that’s valid globally:

We’ve never seen a credit card offer a perk quite this valuable before. Obviously, the spending requirement is massive here, and this would only make sense if you were planning a lot of travel in a particular year. For a certain type of consumer, though, this is an incredible opportunity.

A few Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card benefits are set to expire on December 31, 2026, so they won’t be around for too much longer. Here’s a quick look:

If you already have the card, now is your last chance to take advantage of these perks. Especially with the 10% transfer bonus, it’s worth seeing if an Aeroplan award flight makes sense with your upcoming travel plans so you can get some extra value for your rewards before this perk retires.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card is an innovative product with a big welcome bonus, great return on spending, and valuable perks. That’s just about all that I look for in a credit card.

Airline co-brand credit cards are extremely popular given the allegiance many people have to a particular airline. Admittedly Aeroplan is at a disadvantage in the US market, since not as many people in the US are loyal to Air Canada as they are to American, Delta, or United, for example.

That being said, I think the thoughtful value proposition of this card more than makes up for it for Air Canada loyalists. If you like to redeem points for international premium cabin awards, it could be worth applying for this card. Similarly, the card can be worth it for the Pay Yourself Back feature, whereby you can redeem your Aeroplan points however you’d like toward a travel purchase.

Hopefully most people find value beyond just the bonus, given the excellent rewards structure.

Arguably the biggest challenge with the Aeroplan Credit Card is how easy Aeroplan points are to earn with other cards that provide more flexibility. Aeroplan is transfer partners with several bank currencies, including Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Chase Ultimate Rewards, and all those currencies can be converted at a 1:1 ratio.

That means the points are pretty easy to come by, and in many cases there are compelling value propositions on those cards as well.

If you’re under 5/24, consider these two cards from Chase:

If you’re over 5/24, these are some other top Aeroplan Card alternatives to consider:

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card is phenomenal, and easily the most innovative co-branded airline credit card we’ve seen. The card offers a nice welcome bonus, a lucrative rewards structure with a variety of incentives for spending, and comes with great perks, like elite status.

The Aeroplan program is rewarding in general, but if you don’t fly Air Canada or book award flights through Aeroplan more than once or twice a year, you might want to consider earning flexible points that transfer to this program instead.

Learn more about the Aeroplan Credit Card.

It's just too bad the partner awards have really dried up. 3x earn rate on travel is decent, but with an occasional transfer bonus the 2x rate on Sapphire Preferred becomes 2.5x if you really want Aeroplan points.

For Canadian residents going for high AC status, ignoring this card will cost you. ALL Accor reward points have a fixed value when you redeem them toward eligible hotel stays: 1,000 points get you 20 euros off. That gives each reward point a hotel stay value of 2 euro cents and is why TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Accor points at 2.25 cents.

ALL Accor reward points expire after 365 consecutive days without eligible point-earning activity. Any qualifying activity that credits at least one reward point extends the validity of your entire balance for another 365 days. An eligible donation of reward points can also extend the validity of your balance.

ALL Accor doesn't price hotel awards as traditional free nights. Instead, you can generally redeem 1,000 reward points for 20 euros off an eligible stay. When redeeming online, you can use 1,000 points for 20 euros off or 2,000 points for 40 euros off; after that, redemption amounts generally increase in increments of 2,000 points.

You can earn ALL Accor Silver, Gold or Platinum status through either status nights or status points within a calendar year. Silver requires 10 nights or 2,000 status points, Gold requires 30 nights or 7,000 status points, and Platinum requires 60 nights or 14,000 status points. Diamond status requires 26,000 status points and can't be earned through nights alone, while Limitless status is available by invitation only.

An eligible stay paid for in part or in full with reward points can still earn status nights. However, you'll only earn reward points and status points on the eligible portion of the bill that you pay without reward points.

Accor may not have the same name recognition or footprint in the U.S. as some other major hotel groups, but its portfolio may be difficult to ignore if you travel internationally. Its brands range from luxury names such as Raffles and Fairmont to budget-friendly options such as Ibis.

The ALL Accor loyalty program works differently from many hotel programs familiar to U.S. travelers. Reward points have a fixed value in euros toward most eligible hotel stays, elite status can be earned through nights or eligible spending, and paid memberships can help you save on stays and accelerate your progress toward status.

Here's what you need to know about earning and redeeming ALL Accor points, qualifying for elite status and deciding whether the program is a good fit for you.

ALL Accor is the hotel loyalty program for Accor Group. The program covers over 5,800 hotels across more than 45 brands in 110-plus countries worldwide, ranging from Fairmont and Pullman to Mercure and Ibis.

Accor has an especially strong footprint in Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Asia-Pacific region. Its comparatively limited North American footprint makes ALL Accor less appealing to many U.S.-based travelers.

You can become a member of ALL Accor by visiting the program's website and clicking the sign-up button in the upper-right corner. From there, it's a quick and easy process to sign up for the free-to-join ALL Accor program.

You'll see two different points balances in your ALL Accor account: reward points and status points. Reward points are what you can redeem for stays and other rewards, while status points are one of the ways you can earn ALL Accor status.

When you book an eligible stay — which generally excludes stays booked through online travel agencies — you'll earn reward points based on the brand, your status tier and your eligible pretax spending, as well as status points based on the brand and your eligible pretax spending.

Specifically, here's how many reward points and status points you'll earn per 10 euros (about $11) spent:

So, a Classic member staying at an Adagio Access property would earn 500 reward points and 500 status points on 1,000 euros of eligible pretax spending, while a Diamond elite member would earn double the reward points but the same number of status points. Meanwhile, 1,000 euros of eligible pretax spending at a Fairmont would earn 2,500 status points regardless of elite tier, but a Classic member would earn 2,500 reward points while a Diamond elite member would earn 5,000 reward points.

Accor has more than 45 brands; here's an overview of the Accor Group brands:

However, not all of these brands participate fully in ALL Accor. The list of excluded hotels and brands is rather long, but note that no HotelF1 properties participate, most Ibis Budget properties are excluded and only select The Hoxton hotels participate.

ALL Accor also includes select third-party “Partner of ALL Accor” properties. Earning and elite benefits may vary at these hotels, and reward points can't be used to reduce the cost of stays at IntercityHotel, Steigenberger, Steigenberger Icon, Maxx, Jaz in the City or Zleep properties.

The ALL Accor hotel loyalty program has an entry tier, four earnable elite status tiers and an invitation-only Limitless tier. Members can also benefit from select paid memberships and occasional status match or challenge opportunities.

Status nights and status points reset at the start of each calendar year. Once you reach a new tier, you'll keep it for the rest of that calendar year and the following calendar year. To retain it beyond then, you must requalify during the next calendar year.

ALL Accor members have Classic status if they don't qualify for elite status. So, as soon as you join ALL Accor, you'll enjoy Classic benefits, including:

You can earn ALL Accor Gold status when you stay 30 nights or earn 7,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Silver elite members, Gold elite members get the following perks:

Some cards issued outside the U.S. offer ALL Accor Gold status as a cardmember perk, though none issued in the U.S. currently do. And Qatar Airways Privilege Club Platinum members can upgrade to ALL Accor Gold status after their first eligible international hotel stay with Accor.

You can earn ALL Accor Platinum status when you stay 60 nights or earn 14,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Gold elite members, Platinum elite members get the following perks:

Once you reach 60 nights or 14,000 status points within a calendar year, you'll earn two suite night upgrades. Each suite night upgrade guarantees a one-night upgrade to a suite. You can earn an additional suite night upgrade for every additional 4,000 status points you earn.

You can earn ALL Accor Diamond status when you accrue at least 26,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Platinum elite members, Diamond elite members get the following perks:

ALL Accor also has an invitation-only Limitless status, which Accor grants at its discretion. In addition to all the Diamond benefits, Limitless members get 24-hour access to a personal assistant and concierge service, can gift Platinum status to a person of their choice and can transfer reward points to as many as five other ALL Accor members (up to 12 transfers per year).

ALL Accor offers three paid ALL Accor+ memberships: ALL Accor+ Explorer, ALL Accor+ Voyager and ALL Accor+ Ibis.

These subscriptions offer discounts, a boost toward higher elite status and various other perks. Although ALL Accor+ subscriptions can be combined, ALL Accor caps the bonus status nights you can receive from subscription programs and cobranded cards at 30 per account, per calendar year.

I've considered buying the ALL Accor+ Ibis membership, as its 15% discount could cover the 99-euro annual fee once you spend about 660 euros on eligible stays booked at the subscription rate.

You have many opportunities to earn reward points and status points with Accor. Here's an overview of the options most relevant for U.S. residents.

When you book an eligible stay — which excludes stays booked through online travel websites — you'll earn reward points based on the brand, your status tier and your eligible pretax spending, plus status points based on the brand and the cost of your stay. Specifically, Classic members earn reward points and status points as follows:

Elite members earn additional reward points on top of what Classic members earn; Silver members get 24% additional reward points, Gold members get 48% additional reward points, Platinum members get 76% additional reward points, and Diamond and Limitless members get 100% additional reward points. However, elite members don't earn any additional status points over what Classic members earn.

So, while a Classic member would earn 1,250 reward points and 1,250 status points on 1,000 euros of eligible pretax spending on an Ibis stay, a Platinum member would earn 2,200 reward points and 1,250 status points on the same stay.

You'll earn reward points and status points not just for your room but also for meals, minibar, spa and other eligible charges to your room. Plus, if you opt to Skip the Clean, you'll earn 100 reward points per day skipped. And keep in mind that you can earn reward points — but not status points or nights — on day rooms at participating Accor properties.

You can earn reward points on rental cars from three partners as follows:

You can earn reward points by clicking through the Collections site before shopping.

You can earn up to 600 reward points on your first survey with Club Opinions. And with e-Rewards, you can earn 250 reward points on your first survey.

You can convert the following transferable rewards into ALL Accor reward points as follows:

Transfers are final, though, so make sure converting your rewards to ALL Accor is the best-value option before you transfer.

Related: Why transferable rewards are worth more than airline miles and hotel points

You can earn reward points as follows when you convert select types of airline and train loyalty program rewards:

After linking your ALL Accor account with an eligible airline loyalty account, you may be able to earn reward points on select flights in addition to the rewards you earn with the airline program. For example, you can earn 1 reward point per $2 spent on eligible Qatar Airways flights and 1 reward point per 2 euros spent on eligible Air France-KLM flights.

Elite members with Gold status or higher in ALL Accor or Qantas Frequent Flyer can earn 1 reward point per 4 Australian dollars (about $3) spent on eligible Qantas flights, while ALL Accor members with Silver status or higher and Azul Fidelidade members with Diamante status can earn 1 reward point for every 7.50 euros spent on eligible Azul flights.

You can earn 1 reward point and 1 status point per 2 euros spent when you host a group of at least eight attendees (or at least eight rooms) at a participating hotel. It doesn't matter whether your event is a professional gathering or personal celebration.

You have plenty of options for redeeming Accor points. As with earning, we'll focus on redemptions most relevant to U.S. residents.

ALL Accor lets you redeem 1,000 reward points for 20 euros off an eligible stay at a participating hotel. You can use points toward part or, in some cases, all of your stay, although some prepaid rates require a portion to be paid by card.

To redeem points for a hotel stay online, log in to your ALL Accor account and search for a stay as normal. When you choose a rate at a specific hotel, look for one with a purple "Pay with your points" designation if you want to redeem points for part or all of your stay.

Near the end of the booking process, you can opt to redeem points toward your stay. For example, I could redeem 1,000 points for 20 euros off my stay and pay the remaining balance with a credit card.

These hotel stay redemptions provide a fixed value of 2 euro cents per point, so you generally won't get outsize value from your reward points.

You can redeem — and, in some cases, bid — Accor points for select entertainment, dining and sports experiences through the ALL Limitless Experiences page. There are some great deals to be found, too, such as this Christmas Eve dinner for just 600 points.

You can also redeem Accor points for select activities through ALL Accor Activities & Events.

It's worth checking both of these programs periodically to see whether any experiences fit your upcoming schedule and tastes.

You can redeem your Accor reward points for select types of airline and train loyalty program rewards as follows:

I don't usually recommend transferring hotel points to other travel loyalty programs, as you'll typically lose a good bit of value. Check TPG's valuations and calculate your redemption rate before transferring ALL Accor points to another program.

ALL Accor is most compelling for travelers who frequently visit Europe, the Middle East, Africa or the Asia-Pacific region, where Accor has a much larger footprint than in North America. Its hotel redemptions are also easy to understand: 1,000 reward points generally get you 20 euros off an eligible stay.

However, that simplicity means you generally won't find the outsize hotel redemptions that are possible with programs that use award charts or dynamic pricing. ALL Accor also lacks a U.S.-issued cobranded credit card, and its U.S.-accessible transfer partners generally transfer at less than a 1:1 ratio.

Elite status can still be useful, especially at the Platinum and Diamond levels, which offer perks such as lounge access, suite night upgrades and complimentary breakfast in certain regions or on certain days. Finally, ALL Accor+ subscriptions may be useful for some travelers.

ALL Accor probably won't be the best primary hotel program for most U.S.-based travelers given its relatively limited North American footprint, lack of a U.S.-issued cobranded card and less-than-1:1 transfer ratios. But it may be useful if you frequently stay at Accor brands in Europe, the Middle East, Africa or the Asia-Pacific region.

Reward points are easy to use at a fixed value toward eligible hotel stays, while higher elite tiers offer potentially valuable benefits such as lounge access, suite night upgrades and complimentary breakfast. Frequent Accor guests should consider whether an ALL Accor+ subscription could pay for itself through discounts, status nights and other benefits.

Even if you don't plan to pursue status, it's worth joining ALL Accor before your next eligible stay to access member rates and earn reward points.

#6062. KLM Offloaded A Passenger Rather Than Use The Blocked Seat We Offered

I recently flew KLM from Amsterdam to Barcelona, and a passenger was taken off our full flight even though my wife and I offered him the empty seat between us. The crew followed a rule exactly, and as far as I can tell, nobody got anything out of it.

Business class inside Europe is basically a regular economy seat with the middle seat blocked. On some planes the middle seat is physically blocked with a small table. On this flight it was just empty, blocked online so nobody could book it, but technically a regular seat anyone could sit in.

I was on KL1519 on 2 September, in row 2 with my wife, with that empty middle seat between us.

After the doors closed, it turned out that two passengers had boarding passes for the same seat. Whoever got there first sat down. The other one was a fairly young guy, and now he had nowhere to sit. The flight was completely full, there wasn’t a single free seat in economy.

I heard the crew apologizing to him and saying they would have to take him off the plane and put him on the next flight.

I knew this would take a while, because the doors were already closed and he had boarded. Getting him off meant opening the doors again, and maybe taking his bag off too. Once on another flight someone got off and everyone had to hold up their bags.

And I felt sorry for the guy. Maybe he was in a hurry to get somewhere, and none of this was his fault. The airline gave two people boarding passes for one seat, and he was already on board.

So I asked my wife if she minded giving up the empty seat between us. The flight is only about two hours. She was fine with it, so I went to the crew and offered it.

The crew was very grateful, but said seating someone there was against the rules and they couldn’t decide it themselves, they had to check with someone.

That took about 10 minutes. Then they came back, thanked me again, and said that unfortunately it wasn’t possible under the rules.

So they opened the doors and offloaded the guy, I hope they rebooked him on the next one. In the end we pushed back about 40 minutes late and landed in Barcelona about half an hour late. After landing I think even the captain came over, shook my hand and thanked me.

As I understand it, the middle seat is blocked to give the business class passengers more space. In this case that was us, and we were the ones offering to give that space up.

We didn’t need the space, and we’d have put up with one more person in the row for two hours.

On a completely full KLM flight, two passengers got boarding passes for the same seat. My wife and I offered the empty blocked seat between us in business, so he wouldn’t have to get off. The crew checked with someone, the answer was no, and he was offloaded anyway, and we left about 40 minutes late.

I get that the crew couldn’t make this call themselves. Still, we didn’t need that seat at all.

Is there a good reason for this rule that I’m missing?

I suspect unfortunately this was one of those situations where "the rules are the rules," and that's that, and it might've literally been a system limitation. Perhaps they couldn't figure out how to technically show someone as being "loaded" on the flight, given that the middle seats don't have a corresponding seat in the system. As far as the GDS knows, those middle seats aren't blocked, but instead, they just don't exist. But you're of course absolutely right, in the end there was a substantial delay, and this could've been avoided.

#6061. “Level 3 Threat”: American Airlines Flight To Chicago Diverts After Cockpit Breach Attempt

An American Airlines flight traveling from San Diego International Airport (SAN) to Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) was diverted to Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX) overnight following a serious onboard security incident. According to ABC 15 Arizona, air traffic controllers reported a "Level 3 threat" aboard the aircraft, with cabin crew and passengers restraining a disruptive passenger before the aircraft landed safely.

While initial reports suggested that the passenger attempted to breach the cockpit, according to AIRLIVE, police have yet to confirm which aircraft door was targeted. Federal regulations impose strict requirements on airlines to safeguard their flight decks, and several passengers who have attempted to gain unauthorized access to cockpits in recent years have subsequently been sentenced to federal prison and substantial fines.

AA1494 departed San Diego late on Tuesday evening, and according to flight tracking data, the overnight service was operated by an Airbus A321 registered N568UW, according to Planespotters.net. The 13-year-old aircraft originally entered service with US Airways before joining American's fleet after the merger of the two carriers.

The Phoenix Police Department said preliminary findings indicated that a male passenger had disregarded repeated instructions from flight attendants and attempted to interfere with an aircraft door. Initially, this was reported as an attempted breach of the cockpit door, but subsequent ATC recordings obtained via X suggest the unruly passenger might have tried to open door R in the forward cabin, triggering an alarm. Authorities have yet to confirm whether it was one or both of these doors.

Video footage recorded by passengers showed the individual being restrained, while police confirmed that both passengers and crew members were involved in subduing him.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) confirmed that the aircraft landed safely in Phoenix, where law enforcement officers removed the passenger. It also said that the FBI has been notified of the incident and confirmed that it will investigate. According to Arizona's Family, the individual was taken to the hospital with a minor injury, while no other injuries were reported.

“We want to thank our team members for their professionalism, as well as our customers for their assistance and understanding,” American said in a statement.

The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) classifies onboard security threats into four levels of increasing severity. In February 2026, the International Federation of Air Line Pilots' Associations (IFALPA) and the International Federation of Air Traffic Controllers' Associations (IFATCA) called for wider adoption of the framework to improve coordination between airlines, flight crews, air traffic controllers, and law enforcement agencies.

Physical aggression toward other occupants

Attempted or actual unauthorized cockpit entry

Notably, an attempted cockpit breach would ordinarily constitute a Level 4 threat, and the fact that ATC reported a Level 3 threat further supports the theory that the unruly passenger was tampering with door R. Either way, it represented an unacceptable risk to the aircraft and its passengers, which fully supports the pilot's decision to divert.

According to the FAA, the captain is responsible for the safety of the aircraft, its passengers, and crew. Federal regulations also grant captains considerable emergency authority, including the ability to deviate from standard operating procedures when necessary to safeguard the aircraft. While publicly available regulations do not mandate an automatic diversion for every threat classification, captains will usually divert when continued flight presents an unacceptable safety risk.

The crew declared an emergency as a result of the incident.

American experienced a similar incident in February 2022, when AA1775 from Los Angeles to Washington, DC, diverted to Kansas City. According to the Associated Press (AP), the passenger attempted to access the cockpit and open an aircraft exit. In July 2024, Juan Rivas was sentenced to 19 months in federal prison and ordered to pay American Airlines $64,434 in restitution.

$7,500 fine, civil penalties and three years of supervised release

Over $73,000 restitution and one year of supervised release

One of the most recent convictions involved a Swiss International Air Lines flight that returned to Newark in March 2024 following an attempted cockpit breach and assaults on cabin crew. In June 2026, Belgian passenger Jan Daeninck was sentenced to 10 months in prison. The case also highlights the considerable financial consequences for offenders, with Daeninck ordered to pay more than $73,000 in restitution.

While the federal prison sentences in these four recent cases ranged from 10 to 19 months, US law allows for considerably harsher punishment. Interference with flight crew members through assault or intimidation carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison, with even more severe penalties possible under certain circumstances. Whether the passenger aboard AA1494 faces federal prosecution will depend on the findings of the ongoing investigation.

#6060. Malaysia Airlines Orders Up To 16 Boeing 787-10s, Deliveries Start 2032

Malaysia Airlines has just placed a new aircraft order, as the airline will be adding a new wide body aircraft type to its fleet. This seems logical enough, even if the carrier’s long haul fleet seems rather diversified at this point.

Malaysia Airlines has placed its first-ever Dreamliner order, as the airline will be taking delivery of up to 16 Boeing 787-10s. This includes a firm order for 10 jets, plus options for six more, with deliveries expected between 2032 and 2035.

For context, the 787-10 is the largest variant of the Dreamliner. While it has the least range of any 787 variant, the per-seat economics are great, given how it’s “stretched.” While some airlines have started to use the 787-10 for high capacity regional routes, Malaysia Airlines is taking a different approach.

The oneworld carrier intends to use these planes to support its long haul fleet modernization and international expansion, including routes to Europe, along with destinations throughout Asia-Pacific. The airline points out how long haul demand to and from Southeast Asia has increased by more than 50% over the past decade.

Here’s how Malaysia Airlines Group CEO Nasaruddin Bakar describes this:

“The acquisition of the 787 Dreamliner represents a strategic investment in the future of Malaysia Aviation Group. As we look ahead to the next phase of growth, these aircraft will strengthen our ability to serve key international markets with greater capacity, efficiency and flexibility, while delivering the elevated travel experience our customers expect. Beyond fleet renewal, this investment reinforces our commitment to maintaining a modern, competitive airline that supports Malaysia’s connectivity and global aspirations.”

For context, Malaysia Airlines currently has a fleet of just over 90 aircraft, with another 75 aircraft on firm order. As it stands, Malaysia Airlines has:

Now the airline has the following planes on firm order:

A few things stand out here. First of all, it’s cool to see Malaysia Airlines growing again, after a rather rough… what, nearly 15 years? At this point the airline has enough planes on order to both replace its previous generation fleet, and expand. I’d expect the 16 A330ceos will be retired at some point in the coming years, and more than replaced by the A330neos that remain on order. Furthermore, the 737-800s will all be replaced by the 737 MAXs.

The 787-10 is an incredible plane in terms of economics, especially as Boeing has been able to make incremental range improvements, turning it into a true long haul aircraft.

At the same time, I can’t help but feel like it’s unusual how the airline has just seven A350s, with no more on order, and is now switching to the 787 for fleet renewal. Admittedly the A350 was ordered back in the day under a completely different management team, which also at one point thought the A380 was a good fit for the airline.

So I am curious how the carrier’s fleet evolves. Will the seven A350s stick around, or will they eventually just be replaced by 787-10s? Even with airspace restrictions and headwinds, it seems like all of Malaysia Airlines’ routes should be within range for the 787-10, though admittedly London (LHR) might be on the cusp, depending on how airspace closures evolve, how dense of a configuration the airline selects, etc.

The big challenge with the airline industry is that it’s never static, and decisions aren’t made in a vacuum. One management team makes one decision, and then a management team later on can’t just undo what the other management team did, without it being costly. So I get that they’re doing what they can…

Malaysia Airlines is the newest customer for the Boeing 787, as the airline has ordered up to 16 787-10s, including 10 firm orders and six options. The airline plans to use this for a long haul expansion to Europe, as well as for flights in Asia-Pacific.

It’s cool to see Malaysia Airlines continuing to grow, as the carrier has quite the order book at this point. I am curious if the airline keeps around the seven A350s in the long run, or how the airline manages its three wide body aircraft types.

What do you make of Malaysia Airlines’ Boeing 787-10 order?

#6058. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

“Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”

“Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”

Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

“The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

“As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

“While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

“I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”

Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”

“I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.
