I added the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card to my wallet over 10 years ago for its simple earning rates and modest $95 annual fee.

It has remained a valuable mid-tier travel rewards card due to its straightforward earning rates and no foreign transaction fees. Plus, you have multiple ways to redeem your rewards, including covering recent travel purchases at a fixed rate and transferring your miles to any of the 15-plus Capital One airline and hotel partners.

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

The Capital One Venture Rewards offers at least 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase, making it an excellent everyday spending card. Plus, it offers 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel. These earning rates make the Capital One Venture Rewards card an appealing and good option for consumers who want to use one card for all their purchases.

Unlike many of the other best everyday spending cards, the Venture Rewards card stands out by offering no foreign transaction fees. The card carries a $95 annual fee but offers a $50 experience credit on every Lifestyle Collection booking, complimentary Hertz Five Star status and up to a $120 statement credit (every four years) when you use your Venture card to apply for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck. Plus, cardholders enjoy price prediction and free price drop protection when booking flights through Capital One Travel.

The Capital One Venture Rewards earns miles that you can redeem for travel, cash back, gift cards, experiences and more. But you can also transfer your miles to 15-plus travel loyalty programs, including Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue and Choice Privileges.

Related: 7 reasons to get the Capital One Venture Rewards card

Related: Why I keep the Capital One Venture Rewards card in my wallet

The Capital One Venture Rewards offers cardholders several benefits that help offset the card's $95 annual fee.

One of my favorite benefits of the Capital One Venture Rewards is the price prediction and free price drop protection that's available when I book flights through Capital One Travel.

The price prediction appears anytime you search for a flight through Capital One Travel. It provides guidance on whether to book now and also estimates how pricing is likely to change if you wait to book.

If the price prediction advises booking now, Capital One Travel will automatically apply price drop protection to that purchase at no additional charge. Then, you'll receive up to $50 of the difference back if the price drops within 10 days.

These two features often give me the confidence I need to book or continue to track prices. I've gotten money back on several flights via the automated price drop protection, which is always a nice surprise.

You also have some protection if you book a flight, hotel or rental car through Capital One Travel and then find a better price for the same flight, hotel or rental car on another site within 24 hours of booking. Specifically, you can call Capital One Travel, submit a price match claim and then get a travel credit for the difference if the agent can verify the lower price.

I've successfully done price match guarantees for several flights, with the phone calls often taking under 10 minutes. Keep in mind, though, that the itinerary must be an exact match to what you booked on Capital One Travel, and you must submit your claim within 24 hours of making your reservation through Capital One Travel. The price must be in dollars and available to the general public without any coupons, promotions or member discounts.

Capital One Venture Rewards cardholders receive up to a $120 statement credit for the application fee for either Global Entry or TSA PreCheck (every four years). The credit will apply to whichever program is applied to first, so consider your application timing if you plan to pay for applications to both programs with your card.

I love having Global Entry, as it lets me get through U.S. immigration queues quickly, and it also gives me TSA PreCheck. I'd pay the Global Entry application fee even if my Capital One Venture Rewards card didn't offer a statement credit, so this perk effectively gives me up to $120 back (every four years).

Capital One Venture Rewards cardholders can enroll in complimentary Hertz Five Star status through the "Benefits" tab of the Capital One website or mobile app. However, it may take up to 72 hours after you register for Hertz status for the upgrade to take effect, so don't wait until you're about to pick up your rental car to register.

I like having Hertz Five Star status, as it provides upgrades when available, 25% more points and a wider choice of vehicles at Ultimate Choice locations.

Each time you make an eligible Lifestyle Collection booking through Capital One Travel, you'll get a $50 experience credit to enjoy during your stay. The booking must be made in the cardholder's name, and the cardholder must be staying on the eligible booking.

If you are staying at a hotel, the hotel will apply the credit at checkout to qualifying charges up to $50. Ask the hotel which purchases qualify, then charge them to your room.

If you're staying at a vacation rental, the host will apply the credit when you book an eligible experience with a Capital One credit card. However, at some vacation rental properties, you may get the experience credit as a gift card.

You'll also enjoy other perks on eligible Lifestyle Collection stays, including complimentary Wi-Fi, early check-in and late checkout. However, early check-in and late checkout are only provided when available, and bookings may have a minimum stay requirement. At hotels, you are also eligible for a room upgrade (subject to availability).

Capital One Venture Rewards cardholders also get access to Capital One Dining and Capital One Entertainment.

The entertainment platform may be your ticket to cardholder-only VIP packages and hard-to-secure tickets to popular games, concerts and shows.

Meanwhile, the dining platform can help you secure hard-to-get reservations at top restaurants and provide access to exclusive dining events.

Related: Is the Capital One Venture Rewards card worth it?

Capital One miles are easy to earn and redeem yet still offer significant value. Here's what you should know about earning and redeeming Capital One miles.

The Capital One Venture Rewards offers simple-to-remember earning rates. Specifically, you'll earn 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel and 2 miles per dollar spent on all other purchases.

These earning rates make the Capital One Venture Rewards an excellent option, whether it's your only card or you use it primarily for purchases that wouldn't earn bonus rewards on other cards. I often use my Capital One Venture Rewards for purchases that would earn just 1 point or mile per dollar spent if I used another rewards credit card.

One of the big positives of the Capital One Venture Rewards is the flexibility of its miles. However, the two best ways to redeem Capital One miles are to cover recent travel purchases and to transfer miles to select airline or hotel loyalty programs.

Redeeming Capital One miles to cover recent travel purchases gives you 1 cent per mile and is incredibly easy. Once you make an eligible travel purchase with your card, you'll have 90 days to log into the Capital One app or website and redeem rewards to cover your purchase.

However, I prefer to redeem my miles by transferring them to the 15-plus Capital One airline and hotel program partners. Some of my favorite options include Air France-KLM Flying Blue, Air Canada Aeroplan and Avianca LifeMiles, but you also have access to JetBlue TrueBlue, Wyndham Rewards and many other programs.

I recently redeemed 80,000 Air Canada Aeroplan points (plus $85 in taxes and fees) to fly business class from Cape Town to Perth, Australia, on an itinerary that would have otherwise cost over $2,200.

As long as you get more than 1 cent per mile when transferring miles to partners, this is the most valuable redemption option. However, TPG's November 2026 valuations peg the value of Capital One miles at 1.85 cents each. So, you'll usually want to choose airline or hotel programs that offer at least this much value for your miles when you transfer them.

The Capital One Venture Rewards won't be the right card for everyone. Here are some drawbacks to keep in mind:

If the lack of airport lounge benefits and potential difficulty in offsetting the annual fee are your primary concerns about the Capital One Venture, it may be worth considering the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card instead.

The Capital One Venture X has a higher annual fee ($395) than the Venture ($95), but it offers $300 in annual credits toward bookings made through Capital One Travel. Therefore, if you can naturally use the Venture X's full $300 annual Capital One Travel credit, it can effectively narrow the difference between the cards' annual fees to $0.

Venture X cardholders also get 10,000 bonus miles on each account anniversary, starting with the first anniversary. Between the bonus miles and the annual travel credit, most consumers will get more value than the card's annual fee each year.

Plus, the Venture X offers 10 miles per dollar spent on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel, 5 miles per dollar spent on flights and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel and 2 miles per dollar spent on all other purchases. Capital One Venture X cardholders also get access to Priority Pass lounges and Capital One lounges.

As such, the current welcome offer is worth considering: Earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases within the first three months from account opening. This is one of the best offers we've seen for this card, and this is your last chance to take advantage of it. According to TPG's valuations, this welcome offer is worth $1,688, including the credit.

Note that Capital One won't approve you for a new Capital One Venture Rewards card if you opened a Venture Rewards or Venture X card and earned a bonus in the last 48 months. Its 2-mile-per-dollar earning rate makes it useful for purchases that don't earn bonuses on my other cards, while Capital One's transfer partners give me the option to pursue higher-value travel redemptions.

The Venture Rewards isn't the right choice if you want airport lounge access or extensive annual credits. But if you value simplicity, flexible rewards and a reasonable $95 annual fee, it remains a strong mid-tier travel card.

#6056. Airbus A380 Fuel Burn: How 4 Engines Shape The Superjumbo’s Economics

This October, the Federal Aviation Administration sent a harsh reminder to Airbus A380-800 operators about the cost of four-engine complexity. After an uncontained high-pressure turbine seal failure caused an engine shutdown and an aborted takeoff, the FAA directed the Engine Alliance GP7200 turbofans, which power many of the superjumbos, to be recalled from service for overhaul. Replacing each sub-assembly costs up to $528,150 per engine, demonstrating how four large powerplants compound mechanical difficulties and high hourly fuel costs.

Emirates refuses to treat the double-decker as an operational liability. During its financial year ended in March, the Dubai carrier posted a record $6.2 billion pretax profit and bought out 29 leased A380-800s outright to keep them flying into the 2040s. The airline's leadership openly acknowledged that the superjumbo was the most profitable asset in its whole fleet, wagering billions on multi-class cabin repairs while almost all other international operators scrapped the type.

Because four-engine aircraft consume almost twice as much fuel per hour as a contemporary twinjet and require twice as many shop visits when external maintenance facilities stop, most airline planners steer clear of these aircraft. Emirates packs high-paying fliers into slot-choked international airports where additional daily flights are not feasible, turning an out-of-production giant into its top earner nonetheless.

An Airbus A350-1000 consumes 1,823 gallons (6,900 liters) of jet fuel per hour, whereas four Rolls-Royce Trent 900 or GP7200 turbofans consume about 4,600 gallons (17,413 liters). By cramming up to 600 passengers into slot-rationed hubs like London Heathrow and New York-JFK, Emirates reverses that fuel penalty. At slot-capped airports where Emirates cannot get a second takeoff slot, a single 85%-full A380 carries nearly twice as many high-fare passengers as one 787-9, easily paying for the extra fuel.

While small subfleets decimated rivals in Europe, Dubai's fleet size made it viable. Clark said in November 2019, according to Airline Ratings:

"The A380 was a misfit for Air France. They never scaled, they only have ten aircraft. Yes, we faced the same teething problems, but we dealt with them because we were scaled enough to deal with it. If you've got a sub fleet of 10 it's a bloody nightmare and the costs go through the roof."

Running over a hundred quadjets in-house spreads fixed tooling and spare-engine costs over a large number of daily flying hours. Nonetheless, four engines penalize timetables whenever external repair shops fail. By October, 24 Emirates superjumbos had been parked and seven stored due to engine overhauls, while 84 had flown, exposing an older rift within Dubai's dual-engine sourcing policy that helped doom the assembly line.

Emirates powered its first 90 Airbus A380-800s with GP7200 engines before stunning manufacturers in April 2015 with a $9.2 billion switch to Rolls-Royce Trent 900 turbofans for its final 50 jets. Fine desert sand around Dubai quickly accelerated fan blade wear, delaying deliveries by months and sparking years of haggling that forced Emirates to slash 39 superjumbo orders in February 2019, leaving Airbus CEO Tom Enders without enough backlog to sustain production.

Enders shut down the Toulouse assembly line because selling low volumes below production cost made no financial sense, commenting to NPR: "If you have a product that nobody wants anymore, or you can only sell only below production cost, you have to stop it, as painful as it is." Even so, Clark still campaigns for a modernized A380neo, arguing that next-generation engines and composite wings would cut hourly fuel burn from 26,455 pounds (12 metric tons) to 19,842 pounds (9 metric tons).

Airbus declined until commitments reached about 250 aircraft, despite Clark's insistence that Emirates purchase at least 100 modified superjumbos to enable ultra-long-haul flights from Dubai to Santiago and São Paulo. As MigFlug covered, Clark went on the record, saying: "I'm telling you, we would purchase them if you cross-fertilized A350 or 787 technology into a new A380, which would result in a 25% reduction in operating expenses. A minimum (order) of one hundred is required."

How carriers around the world are filling the jumbo-sized void left by an icon of aviation.

Four engines used to be an airline's best insurance policy over open water, but modern reliability turned that extra hardware into dead weight. Quadjets lost their ocean monopoly overnight when regulators allowed twinjets, such as the Airbus A350-1000 and Boeing 777-300ER, to fly for six hours on a single engine. On almost all long-haul routes, newer twin-engine widebodies also reduce fuel consumption per seat by 25% to 30%, rendering four-engine aircraft obsolete.

Maintaining four intricate turbofans increases mechanical wear on additional turbine blades and fuel pumps, resulting in maintenance expenditures for the Airbus A380-800 exceeding $6,000 per hour and overall operating expenses of $30,000 per flight hour or more. The FAA's October directive regarding Engine Alliance GP7200 engines demonstrated the high expense of those additional parts. The agency warned in the Federal Register:

"Although the root cause is still under investigation, HPT interstage mid-seal clocking has been identified as a contributing factor for the failure... The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in an engine fire and damage to the airplane."

Doubling the engine count also increases a fleet's vulnerability to rare, catastrophic manufacturing flaws. In November 2010, Qantas Flight 32 experienced a massive Rolls-Royce Trent 900 explosion over Indonesia after a fractured pipe wall thinner than 0.02 inches (0.5 mm) shattered a turbine disk and severed 650 wing wires. Seven years later, Air France Flight 66 lost an outboard GP7200 fan hub over Greenland at 37,000 feet (11,278 meters) because microscopic strain cracked the forged titanium.

The compromise on the factory floor that stopped the 747's 21st Century evolution.

Due to weight and simple aerodynamics, two large engines outperform four smaller ones. Compared to the Airbus A380-800's four smaller GP7200 or Rolls-Royce Trent 900 pods, modern twinjets like the Airbus A350-1000 and Boeing 777-9 have enormous composite fans beneath each wing that drive massive columns of slower air with far less drag. Additionally, the wing loses thousands of pounds of structural weight and friction when two engine housings and pylons are cut.

Airbus built 25% of the superjumbo from lightweight composites and cutting-edge metals to counteract the weight penalty of four engines. Engineers constructed aviation's first carbon-composite center wing box, saving 3,307 pounds (1.5 metric tons), and topped the fuselage with GLARE aluminum-glass laminates to stop fatigue cracks. Underneath, dropped-hinge wing flaps sealed trailing-edge gaps, so air flowed smoothly across the massive 261.8-foot (79.8-meter) wingspan during high-altitude cruise.

116-inch (2.96-meter) fan; 14,811 pounds (6,718 kg) dry

74,735 to 80,290 pounds of thrust (332.4 to 357.1 kN); 8.7:1 bypass; 36.92:1 pressure ratio

Pairs nine-stage GE90 core with hollow titanium fan

Higher core pressure cuts per-seat fuel burn 25% to 30%

Massive twin fan diameters replace two extra engine pods

Blending stiff carbon ribs with high-strength aluminum wing skins still triggered a costly cracking crisis in 2012. Tiny assembly gaps stressed internal wing brackets until they split, forcing expensive fleetwide repairs. Airbus executive Richard Carcaillet explained to AIN Online: "The solution involves replacing the current wing rib feet—L-shaped brackets that attach the wing ribs to the skins made with the comparatively new, Alcan 7449 aluminum alloy—with rib feet made from slightly heavier, 7010 aluminum used in the A330."

The outlandish atomic flying colossus designed to be the ultimate Cold War lightning carrier.

Airbus absorbed over $330 million in wing-crack repairs across a $25 billion program that never broke even. Enders admitted to Bloomberg in July 2012: "Airbus thought it understood the properties of the A380 wing materials and the interface between carbon fiber and metal, but found out the wrong way we didn't know everything. It has cost the company a great deal of money and [harmed our] reputation." Yet Emirates turned that troubled airframe into an unmatched moneymaker.

Twin decks give Emirates 5,920 square feet (550 square meters) of floor space, letting Dubai install onboard bars, showers, and upstairs premium economy cabins no twinjet could spare. Clark explained to the Points Guy in 2019: "Why was it that it was Emirates, who took it after Singapore Airlines, that it lit up the planet in terms of showers and bars and big TV screens? We did it for a very well-calculated reason... we had taken a huge risk and huge investment."

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Cash-rich and parts-hungry, Emirates invested $5 billion in cabin refits, bought out 29 leased superjumbos, and agreed in November to acquire six more from Qatar's Lesha Bank. Teardown math drives that buying spree: used A380-800s trade cheaply, while one fresh landing gear set or four serviceable engines cost nearly as much as a complete plane. Dubai is cannibalizing its earliest retired frames for spares as Airbus factory support winds down.

#6055. SkyWest Pilots Do The Right Thing At SFO, Then Get Snapped At By ATC

With the number of close calls we see at airports nowadays, it’s great to see when pilots or air traffic controllers go above and beyond to be observant, and exhibit good situational awareness. So along those lines, here’s a case of a pilot paying close attention to ensure everyone’s safety, and then an air traffic controller being frustrated by that…

YouTube channel You can see ATC has the air traffic control audio and a visualization of an interaction that happened shortly before noon on November 21, 2026, at San Francisco International Airport (SFO).

In this interaction, a SkyWest Embraer E175 operating on behalf of American Eagle had just landed on runway 28L, after flying from Los Angeles (LAX). The pilots were switched to the ground frequency, and that’s when things quickly went downhill:

The SkyWest pilots then continued their taxi, and when they got to the gate, the conversation continued:

When you screw up, I suppose it’s human nature to get a bit defensive, and I think that’s exactly what happened here.

Credit to the SkyWest pilots for their situational awareness here. They were instructed to taxi in front of another plane, and another plane was instructed to give way to them, but never read back those instructions. The air traffic controller absolutely should have caught that, and as a pilot, they 100% did the correct thing by noticing the lack of a read back, and erring on the side of caution.

This isn’t just some theoretical risk, but ground collisions are the most common kinds of accidents involving commercial aircraft. Could the SkyWest pilots have said “we’re holding short because the other plane didn’t read back instructions?” Sure, but it seems like the time gap here was a matter of seconds, and they didn’t want to step on the radio calls of another pilot, in case they were going to read back.

What I think is really unprofessional is how the air traffic controller then responded to this:

The pilots of a SkyWest flight decided to hold short of a taxiway after they observed the plane that was supposed to give way to them not reading back the correct instructions. That was absolutely the right move, and the air traffic controller should’ve caught that.

When the pilots explained why they held short, the air traffic controller didn’t respond particularly well. Then when they asked for a phone number, she said the pilots would be talking to someone else, and she clearly wasn’t having it. But then she was also mad when the pilot explained very briefly what was going on, saying the conversation should happen off frequency… a conversation she wasn’t willing to have!

This is a clear situation where you have two very professional pilots, and one very unprofessional air traffic controller.

#6054. Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care plan if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

Sanders said Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

“If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”

Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”

In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”

Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

#6053. Why JetBlue Is My Favorite Way To Fly Economy Across The Atlantic

I’ve flown back and forth across the Atlantic dozens of times in all cabins, including many times in economy. JetBlue definitely stands out as being my favorite, and dare I say it, the most premium of all the transatlantic economy flights I’ve experienced.

My most recent trip was from Europe to Boston (BOS) for the opening of JetBlue’s newest BlueHouse location. The airline covered my flights for the event, but had no input in this article. I’d like to share some of the reasons that JetBlue’s transatlantic experience impressed me so much.

Economy class meals can seem like quite the downgrade should one be accustomed to the elevated fare at the pointy end of the plane.

JetBlue currently partners with NYC-based Dig Inn for its transatlantic economy-class meals, and they’re far better than average. They also offer products from a range of interesting brands, rather than just your classic soda labels.

Here’s an example of the drinks menu on my flight from Amsterdam to Boston.

Meals are served in these stylish, reusable, matte-black sealed containers. I’d love to see more airlines do more to reduce their waste like this.

I was very happy with my choice of chicken pesto pasta salad as the main course, accompanied by sides of beet and carrot slaw and snap peas with feta. The fresh, flavorful, yet cold dishes were far better than many of the reheated slop I’ve been served in economy before.

I was equally impressed by the breakfast I had on the morning departure back from Boston to London Heathrow (LHR). I went for the Bubly sparkling water again, as I avoid coffee on a plane unless it’s served as espresso. The stuff they pour out of those vats is pretty much just glorified dirty water.

As far as pre-landing light meals go, this pizza thing was pretty good, too.

In addition to the main meal and pre-landing light bite, JetBlue keeps a well-stocked pantry at the back of the Airbus A321LR.

JetBlue has been offering fast, free, in-flight Wi-Fi for as long as I can remember. The same cannot be said for some full-service carriers, which still can’t guarantee a reliable, fast, and free connection on their transatlantic flights.

They’ve also added some fun tech features, like the ability to choose the elements for the main meal service via the IFE screen, even in economy. I think it has a more premium feel than being asked “chicken or beef?”

I’m not a frequent JetBlue flyer, so I couldn’t really make the most of the fun personalization features, such as the option to continue watching the movie where you left off on your last flight.

Being given anything more than the standard pillow and blanket in economy is a rare bonus. It had been so long since my last JetBlue flight in economy that I’d forgotten about the complimentary Snooze Kit.

I prefer to use my AirPods to earplugs, but I did make good use of the eye mask for a mid-flight nap.

I’ve flown over my fair share of narrow bodies on long-haul flights, and I genuinely don’t know why such a fuss is made about them being terrible.

JetBlue’s version of the aircraft has comfy seats, with standard Core (economy) seats having 32 inches of pitch. Another common complaint I hear is that there are fewer toilets. For a plane with far fewer passengers (only 114 in economy), fewer toilets kind of makes sense. I didn’t once find myself waiting in line to use the bathroom on either flight.

For what it’s worth, there are two lavatories for 114 economy passengers, so that’s one lavatory per 57 passengers. That’s a little lower than the industry standard, but not by much. For example, American’s standard 787-9s have five lavatories for 255 economy seats, so that’s a ratio of one lavatory per 51 passengers.

If you’ve only got the budget or the points for economy for your next trip to Europe, I couldn’t recommend JetBlue more. They now fly to eight cities in Europe, the planes are comfortable and modern, and the in-flight food and beverage is top of the game for economy.

#6052. JetBlue Cancels 11 International Routes: See Full List Now

JetBlue is the USA's fourth-largest airline for international service. In November 2026, for example, the carrier has 2,723 departures beyond the US border, equivalent to 91 daily flights. Compared to last November, activity has fallen by 9%.

The international arena is a relatively large part of JetBlue's total offering. In the same month, 20% of services are international, more than double the rate for the US's ten largest operators. However, multiple cuts, including those mentioned in this article, have reduced JetBlue's share from 23% last November.

It is common to compare how things have changed between two periods of time, such as different months, quarters, half years, or years. Cirium Diio data was used to see which international routes JetBlue operated in November 2025 but which do not exist in November 2026.

11 links were identified, most of which existed from New York JFK — historically the airline's most-served airport — and Newark. While they could simply have become seasonal or, at least, focused more on the peak periods, that is not the case. They have all been removed. Moreover, as disclosed recently, JetBlue has pulled out of Antigua, Bonaire, Belize City, and Tulum entirely.

Routes Served Last November But Not This November

Following heavy losses, JetBlue removed many underperforming or less significant international routes network-wise as a part of its JetForward restructuring. Compared to last November, such flights from New York JFK have fallen by a considerable 24%, while Boston (a much smaller station for such activity) is down by 16%. Newark has decreased by 68%, with only one route now served, while Orlando is 29% lower.

Despite the reductions, New York JFK remains JetBlue's number one airport for service beyond the US border. It has 42% of the departures in November, reduced from half 12 months ago. What has really changed is the rise of Fort Lauderdale, at which the carrier is increasingly focusing (internationally and domestically), partly because of the exit of Spirit Airlines.

International flights from the South Florida airport are up 63%, with Fort Lauderdale now accounting for 29% of JetBlue's total, 13 points more than 12 months ago. It is developing a mini-hub, of sorts, between the US and the Caribbean and Latin America. Excluding US territories, 18 international routes are available in November, with more coming in 2027.

One of the two new routes seems to be doing particularly badly, with big changes coming. Find out more here!

Several of the 11 routes were pulled after relatively little time, which is often the case, even without a program like JetForward. If the initial performance is not sufficiently good relative to expectations, and the network contribution is not important enough, it is sensible to redeploy the expensive aircraft to where they may perform better.

New York JFK to San Pedro Sula flights lasted for less than a year, influenced by a very low load factor of just 68.1%. The carrier decided to consolidate on its Fort Lauderdale service, which began in November 2025, with that route's traffic figures rising as a result.

Initial data from the US Department of Transportation demonstrates this. Between November 2025 and the following April, when JFK flights still existed, Fort Lauderdale's average load factor was 62.5%. Ouch. But from May 2026 to August 2026 (as far as the data currently extends), it jumped to 90.1%. Given that more and more lower-yielding transit traffic is probably carried now, yields may have fallen.

#6051. Restored to Calder’s plan, the clouds are spinning again

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

Fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

“It’s totally phenomenal,” he said, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”

It was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

Rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”

“It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he said. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”

It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

“We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he said. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”

Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and said he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

“We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he said. “Nobody got how big this was until it showed up on their doorstep.”

Quilici said he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

“Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy said at the time.

Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

“This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have big pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most important and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement said.

The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

“It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” said Kim Shirley.

In addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

But when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and said he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

“Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower said.

According to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The new clouds, he said, are made of carbon fiber.

“These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he said.

Younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

“I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

“I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he said, gazing up at it.

Is Norwegian Luna the best big new ship sailing out of Miami?

For someone looking for a vessel that feels more refined and upscale than what is typical among big Miami-based ships, it just might be. (Its sister ship, Norwegian Aqua, also sails from Miami.)

As I saw during a week on board in October, Norwegian Luna has an elevated design compared to many of the big new ships sailing out of Miami, giving it an elegance that stands out among the competition.

That said, for someone who just wants the widest array of onboard amusements, entertainment and nightlife that they can find on a cruise ship, the choice gets harder.

Although its large, the eight-month-old Norwegian Luna — the latest in Norwegian Cruise Line's Prima Plus class — is notably smaller than the other big new ships that it is up against in Miami. That means there's less room for the wide range of attractions you'll find on those vessels.

Unlike two of its biggest rivals in the market, Royal Caribbean's Icon of the Seas and MSC Cruises' MSC World America, for instance, it lacks a water park area with multiple waterslides on its top deck (though it does have one large water attraction, the Aqua Slidecoaster). It also has fewer and smaller main pool areas. That's a real strike against it for families with kids, in particular.

As someone who generally prefers more intimate and elegant ships, I know which side of the trade-off I'm on. If it were my money, I'd lean toward Norwegian Luna. It's the perfect big ship for me.

But read on to see if it's right for you.

Unveiled in March, Norwegian Luna is the second ship in Norwegian's new Prima Plus Class of vessels, following the year-old Norwegian Aqua.

These two ships, along with two similar but slightly smaller Prima Class vessels that debuted in 2022 and 2023, are smaller than the ships that Norwegian launched just before them, which is a bit unusual. Most of Norwegian's competitors, such as Royal Caribbean and MSC Cruises, have been rolling out ever bigger ships, loaded with ever more onboard attractions and venues.

Related: Norwegian Cruise Line ships ranked from biggest to smallest

For now, Norwegian Luna mostly operates seven-night voyages to the Caribbean out of Miami on Saturdays, competing head-to-head with new ships from Royal Caribbean and MSC Cruises (Icon of the Seas and MSC World America) that are much bigger.

Those two ships, notably, are 59% and 38% bigger than Luna, respectively, allowing for a lot more onboard venues of all kinds, from decktop attractions to showrooms, restaurants and bars.

On the flip side, Norwegian Luna's smaller size, coupled with its elevated design, generally contributes to a more intimate and elegant feel — a significant differentiator.

I say "generally," as Norwegian Luna's more elegant feel is sometimes punctured by aggressive upselling and extra charges that are incongruous with the ship's overall vibe.

It's not a dealbreaker, but it's off-putting at times and something you need to be prepared for going into a sailing.

Cabins are a strong point on Norwegian Luna. The majority of balcony cabins (the biggest category of cabins on the ship) are surprisingly spacious at 358 square feet, with a clean-lined, modern design and solid storage. I particularly love the bathrooms, which offer larger showers than you sometimes get on mass-market ships as well as a clever pivot door that makes them easy to enter.

Balcony cabins account for about 57% of Norwegian Luna's 1,813 cabins. But there are also 140 oceanview cabins without balconies of various sizes and 424 windowless "inside" cabins that offer a modern design with solid storage.

The latter category includes 73 very small but perfect-for-one solo cabins, known as Studios, in a keycard-access-only solo area with its own lounge — a Norwegian signature. Norwegian has leaned into the solo cruise market in recent years with these exclusive solo areas, and the cabins are in high demand. Book one early if you want one.

Norwegian Luna is also home to one of the line's signature The Haven suite complexes. These are separate, keycard-access-only enclaves found on many Norwegian ships that not only have a wide range of lovely suites but also their own private restaurants, lounges and bars, and outdoor sun and pool decks.

On Norwegian Luna, this complex (tied with the one on Norwegian Aqua as the biggest in the fleet) fills the top four decks of the back of the ship, accessible via its own private elevator. It's truly wonderful. Staying in one of its suites — there are 123, including 25 Owner's Suites that measure up to an astounding 2,100 square feet — feels like staying in a completely different, far more upscale vessel.

Among my favorite features of Norwegian Luna's Haven area is its cozy bar, which offers a much-upgraded bar experience to what you'll find anywhere else on the ship. There are higher-end spirits and creative craft cocktails made by some of the best bartenders at sea.

In addition to the suites in The Haven, you'll find additional suites and penthouses outside the area that also come with extra privileges but not all the perks that Haven guests receive.

Pro tip: If you are sensitive to noise, steer clear of cabins with connecting doors to adjacent cabins (you'll find them noted on Norwegian Luna's deck plans). Even when closed, their imperfect seals will cause you to hear noise from the cabin next door.

Norwegian ships have always been known for a wide range of restaurant choices, and Norwegian Luna is no exception. It has more than a dozen sit-down eateries, ranging from a super-casual food hall to a high-end steakhouse — some quite good for a big, mass-market ship.

Just be warned that the restaurant scene on Norwegian Luna is one of the areas where you'll encounter a lot of upcharges, with both high cover charges for some restaurants and additional charges for individual menu items that can really push up the bill.

Among the priciest eateries on board are Norwegian's two signature restaurants, Cagney's Steakhouse (found on every Norwegian ship) and the French-focused Le Bistro (found on nearly every Norwegian ship). Both have cover charges of $60 per person that rise to $72 per person with a mandatory 20% gratuity; that price can climb even higher if you order an item with an upcharge.

Both are elegant and upscale, and serve quality dishes, as does Palomar, which serves seafood-focused Mediterranean cuisine for the same $60 cover charge. I highly recommend Palomar's whole fish-for-two baked in salt, which is well worth its additional $25 charge ($30 with the mandatory gratuity) — not just because it's a showy dish that tastes as good as it looks, but because it's deboned tableside, adding some tableside theatrics to the evening.

Other extra-charge eateries include Los Lobos ($40 per person), which dishes out Mexican cuisine; Nama Sushi & Sashimi ($50 per person), for its namesake Japanese cuisine; Japanese hibachi restaurant Hasuki ($60 per person); and Thai-centered Sukothai ($50 per person).

All of these have mandatory 20% gratuity charges on top of their cover charges, as does Onda by Scarpetta, which is an Italian eatery ($40 per person) with ties to New York City's high-end Scarpetta restaurant. The latter is one eatery I'd skip, as the cuisine is spotty and the service more rushed than relaxing. (Despite ordering four courses, we were barely there an hour as the dishes were raced out to us one on top of the other.)

For those keeping to a tight budget, there are fortunately plenty of solid included-in-the-fare options on Norwegian Luna, too.

The real standout here is Indulge Food Hall, a casual, multi-outlet venue with separate stands and counters serving tapas, Indian dishes, noodles, vegetarian bowls, barbecue, Latin and Mexican food, and rotisserie items. Some of these items, particularly the Indian dishes (which include chicken tikka made in an actual tandoor oven), are quite good for a free-on-a-ship casual eatery.

Pro tip: If you're sitting at one of the many tables scattered around Indulge Food Hall, you can order from any of the stands and counters via a tabletop tablet. But if you sit at the counter for any particular food outlet, you can only order from that outlet's menu. Pick your seats with that in mind.

A sleeper hit with no extra charge is The Local Bar and Grill, which has both indoor and outdoor seating with a casual diner vibe. It's open around the clock for table-served American comfort food (think: burgers, chicken wings and nachos). But most importantly, for me, it's a calmer and less crowded place for breakfast than the seemingly always-jammed buffet at the top of the ship (more on that in a moment). I loved sitting in its outdoor area on sea days, overlooking the water, for a leisurely eggs-bacon-and-toast breakfast served by a friendly waiter — a much more civilized experience than the buffet.

By contrast, the shiptop buffet called Surfside is an included-in-the-fare outlet to avoid. While a convenient quick-bite option for passengers lounging at the pool (it's right next door), it's too small for a ship the size of Norwegian Luna. It has too few tables, too few food stations and too narrow a walkway along the food stations to be a pleasant experience much of the time it's open.

Rounding out the included-in-the-fare options are two larger complimentary sit-down restaurants, The Commodore Room and Hudson's. Both offer the same dinner menu, with decent, if not always consistent, offerings and pleasant service. Hudson's is also open for breakfast and lunch.

Among the upcharges at both eateries are $20-$30 fees for signature dishes from the ship's Cagney's Steakhouse, such as its ribeye steak ($25). While I'm generally not a fan of the trend toward more upcharges at supposedly included-in-the-fare cruise ship eateries, this does allow for what is one of my favorite dining hacks when sailing on a Norwegian ship: creating an almost-as-good-as-the-real-thing Cagney's steakhouse experience at less than half the price.

I order that ribeye and the always-available Caesar salad (nearly identical to the one at Cagney's except you don't get anchovies on top) and a couple of glasses of the included-in-Free-at-Sea-packages Malbec, which is the very same Malbec offered at Cagney's, and pretend I'm at the latter eatery. The total cost, including the mandatory gratuity, is $30 versus $72 per person at Cagney's.

No matter where you are on Norwegian Luna, you are never far from a bar. There are more than a dozen of them in the interior parts of the ship alone, plus more on the outside decks.

Among the liveliest (and my personal favorite) is the Metropolitan Bar, which stands out for its "zero waste" cocktails featuring such ingredients as syrup made from discarded banana peels. It's bustling every night with live music that ranges from Latin beats to classic '80s rock.

The Belvedere Bar at the top level of the atrium is also hopping with live music nightly, as is the Penrose Bar two decks below. (Musicians play at the base of the atrium not far from it.)

All three of these bars line high-traffic areas and can get busy. For something more tucked away, quieter and usually less crowded, the side-by-side Whiskey Bar and Swirl Wine Bar offer intimate spaces dedicated strictly to their respective namesake pours.

There's also the bar at The Local Bar & Grill mentioned in the restaurant section above, which serves as the casual go-to spot to catch a game over bar bites.

Beyond these, you'll find multiple bars servicing the pool and activity areas at the top of the ship as well as every interior entertainment venue, including the main theater and comedy club. Up at the very front of the ship, the Observation Lounge pairs a full bar with sweeping daytime ocean views.

What you won't find on Norwegian Luna, unlike on some competitor ships sailing from Miami, is a true craft cocktail venue. The Metropolitan Bar comes the closest with its "zero waste" cocktails. But even here, most drinks are quick-made affairs lacking the house-made ingredients, specialty clear ice and precision construction that has become commonplace at craft bars on land.

The Whiskey Bar also has craft elements, including a wide range of whiskeys and knowledgeable bartenders mixing old fashioneds, Boulevardiers and other whiskey drinks with precision. But the venue falls down on things like proper ice for drinks. (They oddly have just 20 large cubes available each night, which disappear fast, resulting in most cocktails coming out with the same small ice cubes found at the basic bars on the pool deck.)

For coffee drinkers, a full-size Starbucks in the atrium rounds out the beverage options.

Norwegian is no longer the leader in big ship entertainment, following cutbacks over the past three years. All the big-name Broadway shows, from "Jersey Boys" to "Kinky Boots," are gone. But it still offers solid entertainment in its main theaters, including the one on Norwegian Luna.

The big crowdpleaser on Norwegian Luna is "Elton: A Celebration of Elton John," a flashy tribute show that strings together John's biggest hits with visual pizzazz that includes elaborate costumes and choreography, special effects and archival footage projected on a back screen. If you're an Elton John fan like me, you'll love it.

The other big show in the Luna Theater, "HIKO: Innovation Meets Wonder," is a moody, sci-fi-themed mashup of custom-scored music, dance, showy costumes, 3D projections, lasers and acrobatics (think high-flying trampoline acts and aerial silk routines). It starts out slow but picks up toward the end.

There's also a rocking Eagles tribute show in the main theater with a full band, which is another crowd-pleaser. There are also more tribute shows focused on Billy Joel and Fleetwood Mac (the former in the smaller Syd Norman Pour House; the latter at the main theater).

And yes, you'll see a theme among the performers Norwegian has chosen for these tribute shows. These are all musical groups that are popular with Baby Boomers and Generation Xers who grew up with them, but have also had a resurgence among younger generations — perfect for Norwegian's wide demographic.

One other notable entertainment option is LunaTique Pop Circus, a bawdy, adults-only, cabaret-style nightlife experience set to pop music, with plenty of audience participation. (If the idea of being pulled up on stage terrifies you, don't sit in the front rows.) It's the only show on Norwegian Luna with an extra charge ($45 per person, including four drinks that get served to everyone as part of the show).

LunaTique Pop Circus takes place in Improv at Sea, an intimate comedy club that also is the place for stand-up comedy on most nights.

While not quite as elaborate as the entertainment on the larger Royal Caribbean and MSC Cruises ships that sail out of Miami on weekends, the above shows have been earning high marks from cruisers since Norwegian Luna debuted and are among the most popular activities on the ship.

Just be warned that, because of that popularity, it can sometimes be hard to get a seat for these shows, which is a common complaint among passengers. With just 752 seats, the Luna Theater is small for a ship the size of Norwegian Luna and fills up long before showtime. Ditto for the smaller Syd Norman's Pour House and Improv at Sea venues, which each can hold just 100 or so people.

If you want a seat for any of the shows, particularly a good seat near the front, head to the venue at least 45 minutes in advance.

Norwegian Luna has a lot to offer on its top decks, particularly in the "family fun" department.

The standout attraction is its giant Aqua Slidecoaster water ride. It uses the same magnetic accelerator system found in modern roller coasters to blast you skyward in a raft that then takes you winding back down a meandering waterslide course. It's both tons of fun and completely free.

You'll find several more fun family attractions tucked under and around the Aqua Slidecoaster, including a 12-hole, high-tech minigolf course where each stroke of your ball is electronically tracked and you get bonus points for hitting certain targets. It comes with a per-person charge of $5 but is well worth it.

Also in this area is The Stadium (free outdoor games including table tennis, bean bag toss and foosball) and the Bull's Eye Bar, which features tech-enhanced darts games.

You'll also find the entrance to The Drop, a terrifying-looking dry slide that spirals 10 decks down the side of the ship. It was a hard pass for me, but try it if you're daring.

Rounding out this area are a pickleball court and Glow Court — a high-tech sports court with an LED wall that lets you play challenging ball-throwing games (just be careful not to hit your partner with a ball, as I did; you might find yourself in the doghouse).

While great fun, these attractions eat up a lot of real estate on the top decks, leaving less room for pool areas. The ship's main pool area, just in front of the Aqua Slidecoaster, feels small for a ship the size of Norwegian Luna (and, indeed, was uncomfortably jammed on sea days during my sailing).

One deck up from the pool is the often-crowded Kids' Aqua Park, where little ones can enjoy water sprayers and mini waterslides.

The solution to escape the crowds (if you're kid-free, at least) is to spend $289 per person for a weekly pass to the adults-only Vibe Beach Club — a separate, keycard-access-only deck-top lounge area that is roughly the same size as the main pool area but limited to just 166 passengers. It is blissfully uncrowded and quiet compared to the main pool area and has its own bar and hot tubs facing the sea.

Pro tip: Splurge for one of the 12 private cabanas at the Vibe Beach Club, which cost a seemingly high $619 per week but come with access for two people, so they're really only about $310 per person. That's just $21 more per person than buying two Vibe passes, and it's a much nicer experience.

Alternatively, you can book a cabin in The Haven, which, as noted above, also has its own decktop lounge area (at the back of the ship) with its own pool and bar.

Between these two areas (Vibe and The Haven), Norwegian Luna notably has a lot more of its decktop real estate devoted to exclusive upcharge areas than other big ships sailing from Miami. What this effectively means is that the ship offers a bifurcated decktop experience. If you pay up, you will experience something more relaxing and exclusive than you will find on many other big ships. If you don't, the top deck experience might feel less appealing.

That said, if you're willing to head down nine decks, you'll find additional outdoor lounge space with lounge chairs and small plunge pools along an outdoor promenade that wraps around the sides of the ships. With a cool South Beach vibe that includes plush circular seats for two surrounded by wading pools, it's an innovative additional outdoor area that is often less crowded than the top-deck pool area.

For indoor fun, the family-focused Luna Game Zone near the Observation Lounge offers an array of video, virtual reality and other games (some for free and some for a fee). Plus, for adults, there's a sizable casino with VIP and smoking rooms, as well as slots and table games.

Norwegian Luna also has a massive, multilevel spa (the Mandara Spa) with one of the loveliest and most relaxing thermal suites at sea. Accessible for an extra charge, it has a stunning, two-deck-high room with water therapy pools; a separate area that is home to all sorts of therapeutic rooms including Finnish, charcoal and clay saunas, a steam room and a salt room; and a separate, blissfully relaxing room full of heated loungers overlooking the sea.

Just be warned that access to the thermal suite costs a sky-high $630 per person for the week (though discounts are sometimes available onboard at the start of the cruise).

The spa area is also where you'll find the ship's fitness room, which is free to use and offers plenty of cardio equipment and free weights, but lacks a full range of weight machines.

The ship's entertainment staff also programs all sorts of daily activities throughout the ship, including trivia games, karaoke, art and dance classes, and family events.

Through at least April 2028, Norwegian Luna will mostly sail seven-night cruises from Miami to the Caribbean, with departures on Saturdays. The exception is during the summer of 2027, when it will reposition to New York for four-, five- and seven-night cruises to Bermuda.

When sailing from Miami, the ship operates both Eastern and Western Caribbean itineraries. Eastern Caribbean itineraries typically include stops at Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic; St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands; Tortola, British Virgin Islands; and Great Stirrup Cay, Norwegian's private island in the Bahamas. Western Caribbean itineraries typically bring calls in Roatan, Honduras; Harvest Caye, Belize; and Costa Maya and Cozumel, Mexico.

Related: Eastern Caribbean vs. Western Caribbean cruises

Fares for seven-night Caribbean sailings start at $549 per person, based on double occupancy. Fares for seven-night Bermuda sailings start at $1,229 per person, based on double occupancy.

Such pricing is for inside cabins on the most offseason dates. You'll pay more for oceanview and balcony cabins and suites, as well as for sailings on more in-demand weeks.

Norwegian Luna is a big new ship that feels more refined and upscale than many of the other big new ships sailing out of Miami. That's in part because of its more elegant design and its (relatively) smaller size. The downside of that smaller size is that the ship doesn't have quite as many onboard attractions — like decktop features, showrooms, restaurants and bars — as some of its competitors.

#6049. British Airways Visa Card Review: Is It Worth The $95 Annual Fee?

The British Airways Visa Signature® Card is one of Chase’s co-branded airline credit cards, and British Airways Club is certainly a popular frequent flyer program, given the overall value of the Avios ecosystem, plus the number of destinations in the United States that British Airways serves.

Who should be applying for the British Airways Visa, and under what circumstances is it worth spending money on it? Let’s take a look at what you need to know about this card, and what the best alternatives are.

Link: Learn more about the British Airways Visa Signature® Card

Before jumping into a closer look at every aspect of the British Airways Visa Card, here’s a high-level view of the card’s key features, perks, and fees:

Here are my thoughts on the biggest British Airways Visa Card pros and cons:

If you’re considering the British Airways Visa Signature Card, its welcome bonus, application rules, and annual fee are all probably top of mind. So let’s start by taking a look at these important details.

The British Airways Visa currently offers the following welcome bonus: Earn 75,000 Avios after you spend $5,000 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

Based on my current points and miles valuations, which put Avios at 1.2 cents apiece, this current bonus is worth about $900. That’s a pretty solid welcome bonus, especially for a card with a moderate annual fee.

The British Airways Visa has a $95 annual fee. This is not waived for the first year, and there’s no additional fee to add authorized users.

British Airways’ credit card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s potentially a great card to use for purchases abroad.

The welcome bonus on the British Airways Visa isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have received a new cardmember bonus on the card in the past 24 months. You are eligible for this card if you’ve had the Iberia Visa Signature® Card and/or Aer Lingus Visa Signature® Card, despite the similarities between the cards.

Chase’s other general policies on card approvals apply as well, including the 5/24, whereby you generally won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more credit cards in the last 24 months.

The British Airways Visa Card has no foreign transaction fees, but does the rewards structure warrant putting spending on the card? It might, but only thanks to additional bonuses offered by the card, which incentivize spending.

The British Airways Visa doesn’t have terribly exciting bonus categories. You earn:

There are lots of great credit cards for airfare purchases and hotel purchases. This isn’t a card I would be putting much spending on unless you’re trying to earn a Travel Together Ticket, in which case it could definitely be worth it. More on that below.

British Airways Club is a transfer partner of Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Chase Ultimate Rewards, so it could make sense to put spending on a card earning one of those currencies if you want to earn Avios at an accelerated rate.

There are lots of great uses of British Airways Avios. British Airways Club has roughly distance based award pricing, and the program offers value in situations where other programs might not. Generally speaking, here’s where I see value with Avios:

British Airways is known for adding large taxes and surcharges to some of its own award flights, so this is worth keeping in mind.

Personally I find Avios to be one of the most useful frequent flyer programs for redeeming points, thanks to the number of redemptions this opens up.

Often one of the big challenges people have with points is figuring out how to pool them since you typically need enough points in a single account for a redemption. A cool feature of the British Airways Club program is that you can form household accounts. This allows you to pool the Avios you earn with up to six other people registered at the same address as you.

This is especially awesome in the context of a credit card welcome bonus, since you can pool a ton of Avios in a single account if you have two people get for the card in a household, etc.

There are some benefits to the British Airways Visa Card that could alone justify having this card. For some people, it will be worth spending money on the card to unlock some perks, while for others just having the card and not spending money on it offers sufficient benefits. Let’s look at what those benefits are, and how they work.

One of the best benefits of the British Airways Signature Visa is that it offers a 10% discount on British Airways flights starting in the United States. To take advantage of this, just book through ba.com/chase10, and use your card to pay while using promotion code BACHASE10.

If you fly British Airways with any frequency, this could cover the annual fee over and over. See this post for everything you need to know about the British Airways Visa flight discount.

If you have the British Airways Visa Card and redeem Avios for a reward flight, you can receive up to $600 in statement credits annually. You can earn up to three statement credits, as follows:

There are some basic terms to be aware of:

British Airways now also offers Reward Flight Saver from the United States, allowing you to redeem more Avios and pay lower surcharges. Getting a further statement credit of up to $200 on that is pretty great.

One of the potentially great perks of the British Airways Visa is that you can earn a Travel Together Ticket when you spend $30,000 on the card in a calendar year.

This companion ticket will be deposited in your British Airways Club account four to six weeks after you’ve completed the required spending.

With this certificate, you can book a British Airways award ticket at the full cost of Avios (plus taxes, fees, and surcharges), and then for the second passenger you don’t have to pay any Avios, but rather just have to pay all the fees.

This also offers a lot of flexibility — you can also use the voucher as a solo traveler and get 50% off the Avios required for a ticket. Your ticket can originate anywhere in the world, and you can even travel on Aer Lingus or Iberia.

This can represent a fantastic deal for first and business class travel, given how much those tickets would otherwise cost. This isn’t for everyone, though it has the potential to represent a good value, and I know it’s a feature that many value.

See this post for everything you need to know about the British Airways Visa companion voucher.

As a Visa Signature card, the British Airways Visa comes with the following shopping and travel protection benefits:

You’ll want to review the card’s benefits guide for any exclusions and rules that apply.

The British Airways Visa Card has a solid welcome bonus, and that could be a legitimate motivator for picking up this card. However, personally this isn’t a card I would use for everyday spending, since you can earn British Airways Avios at a better rate with other American Express or Chase cards. It also lacks a few benefits that many other airline credit cards offer, including a free checked bag and priority boarding.

That said, I absolutely think this card is worth holding onto if you fly British Airways with any frequency because:

There are several Avios currencies, with three belonging to International Airlines Group (IAG) airlines — there’s British Airways, Aer Lingus, and Iberia. There are also two other US-based credit cards that directly earn Avios from these airlines. Specifically, we’re talking about the Iberia Visa Card (learn more) and Aer Lingus Visa Card (learn more).

Which of these cards should you select? They have a lot in common:

The differences mainly come in the form of the perks associated with just holding onto the cards, and also the perks associated with spending $30,000 on the cards in a calendar year:

The best card to select comes down to which benefits you value most. Also, remember that you’re eligible for all three of these cards, should you be interested, so you don’t necessarily have to choose between them.

See here for a full comparison of cards earning Avios.

If you want to earn British Airways Avios, I’d recommend getting a card that earns either Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, or Chase Ultimate Rewards points. Here’s why:

With that in mind, which cards should you consider? Here are some of my favorite Chase Ultimate Rewards-earning cards:

If you’re over 5/24 or simply prefer Amex points or Capital One miles, here are some top choices:

The British Airways Visa is one of the best co-branded airline credit cards out there, in my opinion. The card offers a solid welcome bonus, and it can be worth spending money on the card to earn a companion ticket.

Beyond that, the card can be worth having for the discounts offered on both paid tickets (up to 10% off) or award tickets (up to $200 in statement credits), which can cover the annual fee over and over. That said, the card would be even stronger if it offered a free checked bag and lounge access as benefits — though I’d expect the annual to increase if those were added, especially the latter perk.

When it comes to earning British Airways Avios long term, personally I’d much rather earn Amex, Bilt, Capital One, and Chase points, and transfer them to British Airways. Not only does this allow you to earn points at a much faster rate, but it also gives you a lot more flexibility.

#6047. Delta Air Lines Launches 15 New International Routes: See Full List Now

As the northern aviation winter season is here, airlines are increasingly finalizing their plans for next summer. Initial information for Q3 2027 (July-September) shows that Delta Air Lines is planning 258 daily international departures in the all-important period (double for total movements).

The SkyTeam member's offering is currently expected to be 6% higher than for Q3 2026, with 14 daily departures added. It will be the seventh-highest volume on record for that quarter. However, it is subject to change, as Delta firms up its plan. Still, 15 new and returning routes will help, some of which will be operating in the third quarter of 2027, having not done so in 2026.

For this article, Delta's international network in Q3 2026 was compared to what is planned for Q3 2027 using Cirium Diio data. 15 international routes were identified, eight of which are long-haul. As all markets have already been officially announced, this article simply summarizes what is happening and provides some additional context.

Only routes that have already been disclosed and are scheduled are included. As such, any upcoming new link from Seattle, expected to be revealed on December 2, is excluded. While flights to Singapore have been increasingly speculated, this is not entirely certain. Even so, it is unclear when, precisely, they'd begin.

Medium & Long-Haul Routes: Didn't Operate In Q3 2026 But Will In Q3 2027

A brand-new market. The launch was postponed for half a year. Suggestions that this will be delayed to the second half of 2027

A brand-new market. It'll connect the Texas capital with the hugely important European SkyTeam hub. It'll be Delta's only long-haul route from Austin. Interestingly, flights will arrive in Texas at 4:52 PM and leave at 3:15 PM. Is another route coming?!

Previously served in 2021. Replaces Detroit-Reykjavík Keflavík, which Delta last served in 2026. Delta ended that route shortly after Icelandair did. Boston-Reykjavík Keflavík will be the airline's new shortest route to Europe

A brand-new market. Venice is the largest unserved European city from Boston

A brand-new market. The capital of Greece is the #1 unserved European market from Detroit

New for Delta, but Northwest flew via Tokyo Narita until 2009 using the 747-400. Delta flew to the Philippines via Narita until 2020, just not beginning/ending in Los Angeles

Inherited from Northwest. Delta previously operated until 2020

None of the following links are brand-new, which is perhaps not surprising. None of them are new to Delta's map in 2026, although two links were inaugurated in December 2025. They include Austin to Los Cabos, with Delta joining American (albeit only January, March, and April 2027) and Southwest. In Q3 2027, Delta's offering contributes to that market having a record number of flights.

Many of the entries are markets that Delta already serves. They are simply included because flights did not operate in Q3 2026 but are scheduled to do so in the same quarter next year. In many ways, this is a vote of confidence for a route. Obviously, the reverse (a shorter operating period with fewer flights and less capacity) may indicate problems. Just ask Southwest about one of its links to Alaska.

For obvious reasons, Delta's total flights on the aging, fuel-inefficient, maintenance-heavy, but clearly characterful Boeing 757 have fallen dramatically in recent years. Only 8,455 movements are scheduled on the 757-200 and 757-300 in Q3 2027, down by 60% compared to Q3 2026. Retirements have contributed to this reduction, while nine A321neos were delivered in September and October 2026 alone.

The decrease is due to the domestic market (-67% year-over-year). In contrast, 30% more international 757 flights are planned between next July and September, although this is still far below historic levels. This is not because of the relaunch of service from Boston to Iceland after a five-year absence, as that is just replacing the 757 link from Detroit to the nation. In contrast, Q3 flights from Los Angeles to Mexico City do contribute, although this is only one part of the picture.
